Abandoning an animal or depriving it of food or drink is a crime for whoever owns, possesses or has custody of it, so once you take an animal into your own care, keep it fed and sheltered until its owner, the estate or a shelter takes it. To plan ahead, use the optional animal-care clause (`animal-care-access-vi`), which has the tenant name a person you may let in to care for or remove the animal. At an eviction, the officer executing the warrant must arrange care for companion animals (`edu-no-pet-eviction-fact-sheet-ny`).

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution presumes that an appliance left in a unit is one you supply, or says how to exclude one, so list in the lease both what you supply (`appliances-included`) and anything you leave but will not maintain (`appliances-excluded-il`). An exclusion cannot take away the warranty of habitability: whatever the lease says, you must keep the unit fit to live in and fix conditions that make it dangerous, and that duty cannot be waived. In a multiple dwelling you must also keep the building and every part of it in good repair and provide the fixtures that supply water to every apartment, under the Multiple Dwelling Law in New York City, other cities of 325,000 or more and localities that adopt it, and under the Multiple Residence Law elsewhere (its water-fixture rule covers buildings erected on or after July 1, 1952; older ones must have an adequate supply of water), so never list heat, hot water, plumbing, gas or electrical equipment as excluded. If you will not maintain an item, the safer course is to remove it before the tenancy starts.

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to test a rental building for asbestos or to tell tenants it is there. Once asbestos or asbestos material will be removed, enclosed, repaired or otherwise disturbed, the work is an asbestos project that only a contractor holding a state asbestos handling license may do (an owner doing work in an owner-occupied single-family home is exempt), and the contractor must post or give written notice to the building's residential occupants 10 days before work starts (3 days if the contract is signed less than 10 days ahead, or as soon as practicable in an emergency), keeping a posted notice up until the work ends; interfering with that notice is a violation. Before demolishing a building begun before 1974, the owner (other than an owner of a one- or two-family home who does not direct the work) must have it surveyed for asbestos. The Labor Department's asbestos rules (12 NYCRR Part 56) and federal workplace and air rules, which these rows do not cover, add survey, work-practice and possibly owner-notice duties, so check them before any renovation. Asbestos removal can count as a significant repair when a court weighs a rent increase where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`).

title: Condominium, Co-op and HOA Units
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, New York's Condominium Act says leases of units must include the unit's particulars: its designation and location, the recording details of the declaration, the use the unit is intended for and its common interest (`condo-unit-particulars-ny`). Beyond that, no New York statute requires you to disclose the association's obligations, deliver the declaration, by-laws or rules to the tenant, or sign a statement that you know the condominium law, and a long lease does not entitle the tenant to a resale certificate (New York has no resale certificate statute); this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The by-laws and rules bind you as the unit owner and may govern leasing, so give the tenant a copy of the rules that affect residents and have the tenant agree to follow them (`association-documents-delivery-mi`, `hoa-compliance`). A lease with an option to buy a condominium unit does not trigger the property condition disclosure statement, which excludes condominium and co-op units (`edu-optional-lease-terms-ny`).

title: No Balcony Inspection Statute
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires periodic engineering inspections of balconies, decks, exterior stairs or facades of rental buildings. The Multiple Dwelling and Multiple Residence Laws regulate how egress balconies and fire-escape balconies are built and kept unobstructed, and, outside New York City, the state's minimum rules for enforcing the Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code require local code officials to inspect multiple dwellings for fire safety and property maintenance at least every three years; those rules set no balcony or facade inspection. They do require an engineering inspection of one structure: if your property has a parking garage (other than parking used only by a detached one- or two-family house or by a single townhouse unit, or a garage whose only parking level rests entirely on soil or fill), you must have a professional engineer perform an initial condition assessment (for a garage built on or after August 29, 2018, before its certificate of occupancy is issued; older garages had deadlines from 2019 to 2021), then periodic assessments at least every three years, or sooner if the local code office sets a shorter period, and any additional assessment that the engineer's latest report recommends or that the code office requires because of new or increased deterioration; the engineer sends each report to the code office. Any balcony or deck maintenance rules in the state Property Maintenance Code are in a model-code publication these rows do not hold. New York City requires periodic facade inspections of taller buildings under its own local law, which these rows name but do not research. Your general duties to keep the premises safe and in good repair still apply (`edu-habitability-ny`, `landlord-maintenance-ny`).

title: Tenant Cooperation with Bed Bug Treatment
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires a tenant to report bed bugs, allow inspection or prepare a unit for treatment; New York's bed bug statute puts duties only on you, to give written notice within 72 hours of learning of an infestation to the tenants of the units above, below and next to it (without identifying the infested unit) and to post notice of a common-area infestation (`edu-bed-bug-ny`). Put the tenant's reporting, access and preparation duties in the lease (`pest-cooperation-pr`). You pay for treatment as part of your repair duty unless the tenant, the tenant's household or guests caused the infestation, and local codes, including New York City's, may add rules these rows do not research.

title: Arbitration Clauses (Not Offered in New York)
bodyText: New York courts enforce a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes, but the library does not offer an arbitration clause for New York leases. New York voids lease jury waivers in personal-injury and property-damage cases, voids mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims except where federal law requires otherwise, and bans mandatory arbitration in some consumer contracts; whether each of these reaches a residential lease's arbitration clause has to be settled by the courts. Including an unenforceable clause could also be challenged as a deceptive practice under the General Business Law, which lets an injured tenant recover damages and lets the court award attorney's fees. You may add your own arbitration clause; have a New York lawyer review it, and keep eviction cases, small claims and discrimination claims in court.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, or sets an age or condition test for carpet charges. Under the deposit law you may keep money for carpets only as damage caused by the tenant beyond normal wear and tear, such as stains, burns or pet damage, at the reasonable, itemized cost; you may not keep anything for the ordinary wear and tear of occupancy, which routine cleaning after a normal tenancy is. The library does not offer a mandatory professional-cleaning clause: the deposit cannot pay for routine cleaning, and a lease promise to pay for wear-and-tear cleaning risks modifying the tenant's deposit rights, which is void. Record carpet condition in the move-in inspection agreement and the pre-move-out statement (`edu-move-in-inspection-ny`), and use the damage item in `security-deposit-use-ny`.

title: Casualty Exit Waivable, Duty to Re-Rent Not
bodyText: New York treats the two differently. The tenant's right to move out and stop paying rent after fire or another cause makes the home untenantable (if the tenant was not at fault) applies only where no express written agreement says otherwise, so a written lease may narrow or remove it; the library narrows it only modestly and declines to remove it (`edu-casualty-ny`, `casualty-termination-ny`). Your duty to try in good faith to re-rent a unit a tenant leaves in breach cannot be waived: a lease term exempting you from it is void (`edu-mitigation-ny`). Even where the casualty exit is changed, the warranty of habitability still cannot be waived, so rent abatement for conditions you must repair survives.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: New York does not require a lease to say anything about children, but it bars three things: a lease clause requiring tenants to stay childless or not have children during the term (a violation of law), refusing to rent or setting different terms solely because a person or family has children (a misdemeanor, and the family can sue for damages and attorney's fees), and discrimination because of familial status, which covers a pregnant tenant, one with a child under 18, and one seeking custody of a child. A child born or adopted during the tenancy therefore gives you no ground to end it, and your occupancy terms must apply to every occupant alike, whatever their age (`permitted-occupants-ny`). The ban on childless clauses has no exceptions; the rule against refusing to rent to, or setting different terms for, families with children does not apply to one- or two-family owner-occupied houses or manufactured homes, federally subsidized, insured or guaranteed senior housing, and 55-or-older manufactured home parks; the familial-status rule does not apply to renting in an owner-occupied two-family house, renting rooms in your own home, or qualifying 62-or-older or 55-or-older housing, and even those owners may not advertise a preference against children, except for rooms in your own home and senior housing. The federal Fair Housing Act also protects familial status; its owner exemptions are broader than New York's, so New York's narrower exemptions are the ones to follow (`edu-fair-housing-ny`). Local human rights laws, such as New York City's, may protect more and are not covered here.

title: No Cold-Weather Rules on Vacating or Eviction
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires a tenant to give notice before leaving the home empty in cold weather, and none bars or delays evictions in winter or in freezing temperatures. An officer executes a warrant only on a business day between sunrise and sunset, after at least 14 days' written notice (`edu-eviction-process-ny`), and a tenant may ask the court for a hardship stay at any time of year (`edu-eviction-stay-ny`). If you want notice of long absences to protect the plumbing, you may add your own lease clause; keep in mind that in a building covered by the Multiple Dwelling Law (cities of 325,000 or more and places that adopt it), and in a new dwelling covered by the Multiple Residence Law (smaller cities, towns and villages), the duty to supply heat from October 1 through May 31 is yours (`edu-heat-ny`). Local codes may set other rules, which the library does not research.

title: No Collection Fees Without a Court Order
bodyText: Do not put a collection-fee clause in a New York lease. You may not charge a tenant any fee for legal services connected with the operation or rental of a residential unit, and the law counts court fees, attorney fees, notary charges and administrative fees as legal services, unless a court orders the tenant to pay; a lease term to the contrary is void. A collection agency's or attorney's charge for collecting unpaid rent falls on the wrong side of that line, so the library does not offer the clause. Separately, the state debt-collection law bars a creditor from collecting a collection fee or attorney's fee unless it is justly due and legally chargeable. Ask the court for any fees or costs the law allows (`edu-attorney-fees-ny`); a late fee within the cap is the lawful charge for late rent (`edu-late-fee-ny`). New York City's debt-collection licensing rules are local law.

title: Lighting Halls, Stairs and Entrances
bodyText: In a building of three or more apartments, state law makes you light the common areas. Where the Multiple Dwelling Law applies (New York City and other cities of 325,000 or more, and localities that adopt it), you must light every vestibule, entrance hall, public hall, stair, fire-stair and fire-tower on every floor from sunset to sunrise (continuously in fire-stairs and in windowless halls and stairs), keep a light at or near the outside of the front entrance burning from sunset to sunrise, and put a light over the mailboxes where daylight is not enough to read the names. Where the Multiple Residence Law applies (other cities and all towns and villages), you must light every public hall, stair and fire-stair on every floor adequately. You may not make a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric account: a shared meter must be eliminated or put in your name, and only in limited cases may you sign an agreement under which the tenant pays for the apartment's own use alone (`edu-utility-apportionment-ny`, `shared-meter-agreement-ny`). Outside New York City, the state Property Maintenance Code applies to all existing buildings and premises, including one- and two-family rentals, and may set lighting rules of its own; it is a model-code publication these rows do not hold. Local codes, including New York City's Housing Maintenance Code, may add rules these rows do not research.

title: Leases on Indian Nation Lands
bodyText: New York has no communal-land approval system for ordinary private land, but its Indian Law controls leases of land owned or occupied by an Indian nation, tribe or band, and a lease made without the approval it requires is void. Examples: Seneca Nation tribal lands on the Allegany, Cattaraugus and Oil Springs reservations may be leased by the Seneca council on its terms; an Onondaga member may lease improved land to outsiders for up to ten years, but no individual member may lease land for commercial purposes, which the statute defines as any purpose other than agriculture for which the land may be used to derive a profit (so renting for income may count), and such leases need a written contract by a majority of the chiefs approved by the tribe's agent; Tonawanda agricultural leases need council approval, run at most a year, and rent paid under a void lease belongs to the nation; and anyone who resides on tribal lands without being a member, an authorized guest or a lessee can be removed as an intruder. Land in the former congressional villages on the Allegany reservation (including Salamanca) is held under Seneca Nation leases treated as a freehold, so the general laws apply there. Federal law also governs Indian land and is not covered here. If the property is on or near reservation land, confirm that your own title or lease and every required approval are in place before you rent it out; these rows do not otherwise address it.

title: No Rent for Unlawfully Occupied or Condemned Units
bodyText: In a building covered by the Multiple Dwelling Law, you cannot recover rent, or evict for nonpayment, for any period the building is occupied without the certificate of occupancy or compliance the law requires; the building is then treated as unfit for human habitation and the authorities must have it vacated. The Multiple Residence Law has the same rent bar for its multiple dwellings occupied without a required certificate. In multiple dwellings, a rent-impairing violation left uncorrected six months after the agency's notice also bars rent for the affected unit (`edu-landlord-breach-remedy-ny`), and in New York City an owner who fails to register a multiple dwelling as local law requires cannot recover rent until it does. A search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found no separate statewide rule barring rent merely because an agency issues a vacate order; after a casualty the tenant may leave and stop owing rent, and while the home is unusable the warranty of habitability abates rent. Local codes may add their own rules.

title: Confession of Judgment from a New York Tenant
bodyText: New York does not bar a confession of judgment taken from a residential tenant before any claim arises, but it limits one closely, and the library does not offer it. A confession works only as a separate affidavit the tenant signs, stating the sum, the facts the debt arises from and that the sum is justly due or to become due, the county where the tenant lives and, where it applies, that the consumer-debt interest rate applies; a sentence in the lease is not enough. You may file it only within three years after it is signed, only in the county the affidavit names or where the tenant lives at filing, and never after the tenant's death, and for sums not yet due you may collect only what has become due. It gives you a money judgment, never possession: removing a tenant still takes an eviction case. It cannot carry attorney or other legal fees, which need a court order. A confession demanded as a condition of renting also invites a challenge as unconscionable or as a deceptive practice, so take advice before using one.

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have That New York Does Not
bodyText: New York's warranty of habitability is short, implied in every residential lease and cannot be waived or modified, so its gaps are not places to relax. Searches of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none of these: a materiality threshold for defects; a presumption that you breached or delayed; a statutory repair deadline running from a tenant's request; a required habitability statement in the lease; a prescribed way for tenants to give repair notice; a right to end the lease because repairs cost too much; a general repair-and-deduct right; a separate-document rule for shifting chores to a tenant; or a single article-wide non-waiver rule. Nor may a lease trade named defects for lower rent or drop the water supply where there is no utility connection, because any modification of the warranty is void. Each point has its own row, and agency repair orders, the Multiple Dwelling and Multiple Residence Laws and local housing codes still set their own standards and deadlines.

title: Rules New York Does Not Have
bodyText: Many rules found in other states have no New York counterpart in the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution; each absence is explained, with what applies instead, in its own row. Disclosures and paperwork: no radon, mold, meth, sex-offender, foreclosure, code-violation, code-variance, military-zone, ordnance or demolition, shoreline, special-district, property-tax, chemical-warning or state lead notice (`edu-no-radon-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-mold-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-meth-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-sex-offender-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-foreclosure-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-code-violation-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-code-variance-notice-ny`, `edu-no-military-zone-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-ordnance-demolition-meter-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-shoreline-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-special-district-statement-ny`, `edu-no-property-tax-rent-statement-ny`, `edu-no-prop65-warning-ny`, `edu-no-lead-state-notices-ny`); no state rights guide, tenant rights statement or truth-in-renting notice (`edu-no-rights-guide-ny`, `edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-ny`, `edu-no-truth-in-renting-ny`); and no initials, translation, readability, lease-copy, single-family occupancy or fee-transparency rule (`edu-no-lease-initials-requirement-ny`, `edu-no-translation-duty-ny`, `edu-no-plain-language-statement-ny`, `edu-no-lease-copy-rule-ny`, `edu-no-sfr-occupancy-disclosure-ny`, `edu-no-fee-transparency-rule-ny`). Money and terms: no landlord's lien, repair-and-deduct statute, payment-order rule, early-termination fee rule, renters-insurance rule, lease-type parity rule or small-landlord exemption from repair remedies (`edu-no-landlord-lien-ny`, `edu-no-repair-deduct-ny`, `edu-no-application-order-rule-ny`, `edu-no-early-termination-fee-rule-ny`, `edu-no-renters-insurance-rule-ny`, `edu-no-lease-type-parity-ny`, `edu-no-repair-escrow-exemption-ny`). Property and use: no state limit on renting in single-family zones, no health-district rule supply duty, no state recycling notice, and no rule on double letting, EV charging, tenant cameras, displays, foreign ownership, misrepresented assistance animals or domestic-violence lock changes (`edu-no-single-family-zone-rental-limit-ny`, `edu-no-health-district-rental-rules-ny`, `edu-no-recycling-notice-ny`, `edu-no-double-letting-rule-ny`, `edu-no-ev-charging-rule-ny`, `edu-no-camera-rule-ny`, `edu-no-display-rule-ny`, `edu-no-foreign-ownership-rule-ny`, `edu-no-service-animal-misrep-ny`, `edu-no-dv-lockchange-ny`). Absent from state law does not mean unregulated: New York City and other localities may have their own rules, which these rows name but do not research.

title: Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Laws
bodyText: Several rules that bind you sit outside New York's landlord-tenant articles, and the library states each in its own row. Squatters are not tenants and can be removed in a summary proceeding after a 10-day notice (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-ny`); cash and money-order rent needs a written receipt (`edu-rent-receipts-ny`); in Albany, Newburgh, Schenectady and Syracuse an eviction petition must show compliance with the city's rental registration law, and in New York City an unregistered multiple dwelling owner cannot recover rent (`edu-local-registration-ny`). A foreign LLC or corporation doing business in New York without authority cannot bring any case until authorized, and neither the LLC Law nor the Business Corporation Law says whether renting out property is doing business, so get advice before filing; an unfiled assumed name bars suits on leases made in that name; and an out-of-state owner can be sued and served on claims arising from New York property (`edu-entity-landlord-court-ny`, `edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-ny`). No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York was found that makes any person, landlords included, report tenants or tenancies to an agency in a market-rate rental.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: Under New York's Lien Law, a contractor or supplier who improves real property with the consent or at the request of its owner can file a lien, and a tenant with a lease for a term of years counts as an owner of its leasehold. So work a tenant orders can be liened against the tenant's interest, and against yours only if the work was done with your consent or at your request; whether simply allowing alterations in the lease is that consent is decided by case law. New York has no notice of nonresponsibility and no rule that a recorded lease keeps your interest lien-free, and a contractor's advance waiver of lien rights is void, so a lease cannot bind the contractor. The library's optional `no-liens-ny` clause makes the tenant pay for and discharge any lien and says your consent is not a request for the work; `no-alterations` already requires your written consent first.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant or prospective tenant. If you know of a hidden defect that makes the home unsafe or unfit, it falls under your general duty to keep the premises habitable (`edu-habitability-ny`), and concealing a known dangerous condition can expose you to claims that the library does not research. Telling tenants in writing about a known, unremediated defect is the cautious course.

title: No Pre-Set Deposit Charges
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution lets a lease pre-set what you may keep from a deposit for cleaning, carpets, painting or any other item, and none prescribes a tenant notice that would unlock one. You may keep only the reasonable and itemized cost of unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility charges the lease makes payable to you, and moving and storing the tenant's belongings, and in a dispute you must prove the amount was reasonable. A price list in the lease can tell the tenant what repairs usually cost, but it cannot make a figure higher than your reasonable, itemized cost stick, and a lease term that waives or modifies the tenant's deposit rights is void. Use the deductions clause in `security-deposit-use-ny` and put the real figures in the itemized statement. Rent-controlled units, some senior-care facilities and rent-stabilized units follow their own deposit rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or requires you to offer a payment plan. You may agree to one if you choose; write the schedule into the lease. Whatever the schedule, all deposits and advances together may not exceed one month's rent, every installment you receive is held in trust as part of the deposit, and you may not charge a fee for the plan before or at the start of the tenancy. Rent-controlled units, some senior-care facilities and rent-stabilized units follow their own deposit rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Prepaid last month's rent is an advance: it counts toward the one-month cap on all deposits and advances, so you cannot collect a full month's security deposit and last month's rent too, and you hold it in trust until it is applied to that month's rent. No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution lets a tenant use the security deposit as the last month's rent, and none sets a special penalty (like other states' bad-faith presumptions) for a tenant who withholds the last month's rent for that reason. The deductions clause in `security-deposit-use-ny` already says the Security Deposit does not relieve Tenant of paying Rent when due; unpaid rent can then be kept from the deposit after the tenant moves out, with the itemized statement. See `due-at-signing-ny` and `edu-deposit-rules-ny`.

title: No Surrender-Notice Condition on Deposit Refunds
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution lets you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, or on a forwarding address. The deposit is refundable when the tenant vacates, and the itemized statement and balance are due within 14 days after the tenant has vacated; a lease term that adds a condition would modify the tenant's deposit rights and is void. The only statutory effect of short notice is that you need not send the pre-move-out inspection notice when the tenant ends the tenancy on less than two weeks' notice. The forwarding-address sentence in `security-deposit-return-ny` helps you deliver the statement; the statute does not stop the 14 days running if the tenant gives none, so send the statement to the last address you have. Rent-controlled units, some senior-care facilities and rent-stabilized units follow their own deposit rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Disaster-Displaced Guests
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant a special right to house people displaced by a fire, flood or other disaster, or limits what you may do about it. The ordinary rules apply: a tenant may have guests for reasonable, temporary stays (`guest-policy-ny`), and a tenant on a one-tenant lease who (or whose spouse) lives there as a primary residence may also add one occupant (and that occupant's dependent children) without your consent, naming them within 30 days, while you may limit occupancy to meet occupancy and safety codes (`permitted-occupants-ny`). Displaced people who stay on become occupants, not tenants, and gain no right to stay after the tenant leaves without your written permission. During a declared state disaster emergency the Governor may temporarily suspend specific laws by executive order, so check any order in force before acting.

title: Disasters and Emergencies
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution ends a tenancy because a disaster is declared, or sets special rent or repair rules for a disaster; the ordinary rules apply. If the home is destroyed or so damaged by fire, flood or another cause that it is untenantable and the tenant was not at fault, the tenant may move out and owes no rent after surrendering, with prepaid rent adjusted, unless a written agreement says otherwise (`edu-casualty-ny`); a tenant who stays keeps the warranty of habitability (`edu-habitability-ny`). In an emergency affecting a multiple dwelling or multiple residence, you must give police, fire and other emergency personnel who ask the names and contact information of affected residents as listed in the lease (`emergency-contact-consent-ny`). During a declared state disaster emergency the Governor may temporarily suspend specific laws, including eviction rules, by executive order, and charging an unconscionably excessive price for essential goods or services during a market disruption is unlawful price gouging; whether that reaches rent turns on case law, so do not raise rent sharply during an emergency without advice. Local emergency orders are named, not researched.

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda
bodyText: New York has no statute on drug-free housing addenda; the library's New York answer is the illegal-use clause in `criminal-activity-ny`, which makes any illegal use of the property a lease breach and repeats the rule that using the premises for an illegal trade, manufacture or business voids the lease. Selling or manufacturing illegal drugs at the property is that kind of illegal business, so you may recover possession through a court proceeding, and neighbors or public officials can press you to act (`edu-illegal-use-eviction-ny`). The library does not offer the broader drug-free addenda used in other states, because New York's Cannabis Law bars penalizing a tenant solely for lawful adult cannabis conduct and protects certified medical use (`edu-cannabis-ny`). Federally assisted housing may use the HUD drug-free addendum under its program rules, which these rows do not cover.

title: Deposit Return After a Domestic Violence Termination
bodyText: New York sets no separate deposit deadline after a domestic violence lease termination: the ordinary rule applies, so within 14 days after the tenant has vacated you must give an itemized statement of anything kept and return the rest, or you lose the right to keep any of it. You may keep part of the deposit only for the reasons the lease and the deposit law allow (unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility charges payable to you, moving and storing belongings), never because the tenant ended the lease early. Separately, prepaid rent or other payments covering the time after the termination date must be refunded within 10 days of delivery of the tenant's written notice, as long as the tenant has moved out. Where other tenants stay on the lease, the co-tenancy continues unless they consent to end it, and no New York statute says how one deposit is divided among co-tenants or whether the departing tenant's share is due before the tenancy ends; get the departing and remaining tenants to agree in writing how the deposit will be held or split, keep the reason for the departure confidential, and if they cannot agree, have a New York lawyer advise you before you pay any of it out. The termination rules themselves are in `edu-dv-termination-ny`; rent-controlled and rent-stabilized units follow their own deposit rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Orders of Protection: Where New York's Law Sits
bodyText: New York has not moved or renumbered its order-of-protection law, so guidance citing these sections is current. Family Court orders for family offenses are in article 8 of the Family Court Act (N.Y. Fam. Ct. Act § 812 lists the family offenses and N.Y. Fam. Ct. Act § 842 says what an order may require); criminal courts issue them under N.Y. Crim. Proc. Law § 530.12 and N.Y. Crim. Proc. Law § 530.13, and divorce courts under N.Y. Dom. Rel. Law § 240 and N.Y. Dom. Rel. Law § 252. An order can require the abuser to stay away from the home, let a party enter to collect belongings at a set time, and bar the abuser from remotely controlling connected devices affecting the protected person's home (such as smart locks); criminal-court, divorce-court and some Family Court orders can also authorize the protected person to end a lease under the domestic violence termination law. An order binds the people named in it, not you: it does not by itself end the abuser's tenancy or tell you to change the locks, so read its terms before acting (`edu-no-dv-lockchange-ny`). A tenant can use a temporary or final order of protection as documentation for an early termination (`edu-dv-qualifying-documents-ny`, `edu-dv-termination-ny`).

title: Domestic Violence: Documents a Tenant May Give
bodyText: A tenant ending the lease because of domestic violence must give you documentation within 25 days of the termination notice, and may choose any one or more of: a temporary or final order of protection; a police or other law enforcement record, complaint or report; a health care provider's record of treatment; or a written verification from a qualified third party (a law enforcement officer, court employee, licensed attorney, physician, psychiatrist, psychologist, social worker, registered nurse, therapist or counselor, a domestic violence agency worker, or a member of the clergy). A third party's sworn or notarized statement with the required information is enough, and the court system's sample tenant and third-party statements satisfy the notice and verification requirements but are not required. The law sets no age limit on an order or report; its only time limit is the 25 days after the notice. You may not insist on one kind of document over another, and you must keep whatever you receive confidential (`edu-dv-confidentiality-ny`). The rules against refusing to rent to or evicting a domestic violence victim (`edu-dv-eviction-ny`) list no documents at all; the termination process is in `edu-dv-termination-ny`.

title: Submetering Electricity or Gas to Tenants
bodyText: No New York statute requires a lease disclosure when you submeter electricity or gas, and none says in so many words whether a landlord who resells metered electricity becomes a utility. The Public Service Law's definitions of electric and gas corporations leave out power or gas distributed on private property only for the owner's own use or its tenants' use and not for sale to others, while the Home Energy Fair Practices Act, the residential customer protections in article 2 of that law, reaches any entity that sells or helps sell gas or electricity to residential customers. For electricity, the Public Service Commission's submetering rules fill the gap, and they reach the lease. You may submeter apartments only with the Commission's authorization where an order is needed, and only on its conditions. To convert a master-metered rental building you file a notice of intent (or a petition, if tenants would start paying for electric heat) and give each current resident written notice before you file, again when the filing is published, and at least two months before submetered billing starts; that last notice must state that prospective residents will be told before signing a lease that electricity is submetered and that they will pay for it. A building whose apartments have their own utility meters may be switched to a master meter with submeters only on a petition showing demand response, on-site cogeneration or advanced energy-efficiency design. When you apply you also certify that every lease will set out, in plain language, the submetering complaint procedures, the tenant's rights and responsibilities under the Act, and that refunds will be credited to affected tenants (a filing rule amended in 2025 whose current text these rows could not read). Once you submeter, unless the Commission waives a condition for good cause, you may not charge more than the utility would charge a similar directly metered residential customer, or charge time-of-use rates the tenant has not agreed to; you must give tenants the Act's protections and tell them of those protections in the lease or another individual notice; the lease may not require binding arbitration of submetered billing complaints; you must bill within 30 days after receiving the utility's bill and keep billing records for six years; on submeters installed or replaced after January 1, 2014, tenants must be able to read the register or otherwise monitor their own use, and any tenant may get one free meter test a year on a complaint; and no shared meter or cross-wiring may remain. Violations can bring refunds, a rate-cap cut of up to 40 percent or loss of the authorization. These rules cover electricity only; no gas submetering rule was found in the rules read. A tenant whose own utility account also pays for service outside the apartment is protected by a separate statute (`edu-utility-apportionment-ny`), and the general billing rules are in `edu-utility-submetering-ny`.

title: No Required Screening of Building Employees
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to run background checks on superintendents, maintenance staff, doormen or other employees who work in your rental buildings or have keys to apartments. One exception: if you employ your own security guards, you are a security guard company under the Security Guard Act and may employ as guards only people whose valid state registration card you have verified, or for whom you have filed a registration application with their fingerprints, photographs and certification of the required pre-assignment training. If you do screen employees and have ten or more of them, New York's criminal-record law bars refusing or firing someone for a past conviction unless the offense directly relates to the job or employing them would pose an unreasonable risk to property or people, and the Human Rights Law bars asking about arrests that ended in the person's favor or sealed convictions. An employer who weighs those factors in good faith and hires the person gets a presumption that the conviction is kept out of evidence in a later negligent-hiring case. Other employment screening rules, including consumer report notices and local fair chance laws, are not covered here.

title: Tenant Energy Usage Data
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution lets a lease clause by itself authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you, or requires you to benchmark a building's energy use. If you want the data, have the tenant agree in the lease to sign the utility's own release form, and let the tenant withdraw consent without penalty (`energy-data-release-wy`); whether the utility accepts the release is up to its tariff and Public Service Commission orders, which these rows do not cover. Utilities may not sell lists of their customers, customers' electric and gas consumption data is confidential by statute, and the Commission may make rules requiring utilities to protect it from unauthorized or unconsented disclosure, which is why the tenant's own signed release matters. New York City requires benchmarking of larger buildings under its own local law, which these rows name but do not research.

title: Who Can Represent a Business Landlord in Court
bodyText: An individual landlord may bring an eviction case or lawsuit in person, but a corporation or other association must appear by a lawyer, except in small claims and commercial claims cases and in town and village justice courts, where an authorized officer, director or employee may appear for a corporation; no statute extends that exception to an LLC, so the cautious course is for an LLC to use a lawyer. A non-lawyer property manager may verify the eviction petition as your agent but may not appear in court for you, and a landlord acting without a lawyer gets the notice of petition from the clerk or a judge. A foreign corporation or LLC doing business in New York without authority cannot bring any case, eviction cases included, until it is authorized (a corporation must also pay its back fees and taxes), though it may defend one. If you rent under an assumed name without filing the assumed-name certificate, you cannot sue on leases made in that name until you file. In a Multiple Dwelling Law building the owner, any lessee of the whole building and the managing agent must register their names and addresses, and in New York City an unregistered owner cannot recover rent (`edu-owner-identity-ny`).

title: No Separate Environmental-Event Termination Rule
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives you or the tenant a separate right to end a lease after an environmental or public-health event, such as a flood, a hazardous release or a government order to vacate. The general casualty rule covers these events: if the home is destroyed or so injured by the elements or any other cause that it is unfit to live in, and the tenant did not cause it, the tenant may move out and stop owing rent unless a written agreement says otherwise (`edu-casualty-ny`). The library's casualty clause also lets you end the lease if you reasonably decide not to restore (`casualty-termination-ny`). Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, a government vacate order is a ground for removal only if the court finds removal is needed to cure the violation and you did not create the condition (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`).

title: EV Chargers When the Lease Ends
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution says who owns a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the lease ends, or whether the tenant must remove it. Settle it in your written consent: under the lease's alterations clause (`no-alterations`), an approved alteration stays with the property unless you require its removal. One statute protects a tenant's removal right: unless you expressly agree otherwise, a tenant who has a right to remove fixtures or improvements does not lose it by signing a renewal lease without moving out. You may keep part of the deposit only for the costs New York allows, such as damage caused by the tenant beyond normal wear and tear, and you must itemize it within 14 days.

title: EV Chargers: Tenant Requests and Building Rules
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental, or requires you to provide charging at an existing building, so whether a tenant may install one is up to you and the lease (`no-alterations`, `edu-no-ev-charging-rule-ny`). The library offers no New York charger clause: billing a tenant for electricity a charger draws through your meter may be a resale of electricity. The Public Service Commission's submetering rules let the owner of a parking facility used on an intermittent, temporary or irregular basis meter and bill plug-in vehicle charging stations without the Commission's approval or its submetering conditions, but they do not say whether a rental property's parking is such a facility, while submetering the apartments themselves needs the Commission's authorization (`edu-electric-submetering-ny`); sales tax may also apply, a question these rows do not cover. If you allow a charger, you may add your own clause; have it wired to the tenant's own meter where you can, require a licensed electrician and any permits, and keep any extra security within the one-month deposit limit. In a condominium, the association cannot effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict a unit owner's charger in the owner's unit or designated parking space, so if you rent out a condo unit, the association approval runs through you as owner. For new buildings with new off-street parking, the state energy code adopted after December 31, 2026 must require EV-ready wiring and charging stations, with minimum numbers for buildings other than detached one- and two-family homes; buildings that already exist are not covered.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution governs a tenant's charger in a parking area other tenants use, or sets a fee for reserving that space, so it is a matter for your consent and the lease (`edu-no-ev-charging-requirements-ny`). If you assign a space with a charger, state any space charge in the lease or a signed addendum, keep cords out of walkways and drive aisles, and remember that a fee charged before or at the start of the tenancy, other than rent and the deposit, is barred. The rules New York does have for chargers in common areas apply only to condominium associations and unit owners, who must get the association's approval and meet conditions such as a licensed contractor and liability insurance. The state rule that only an electric vehicle connected to the charger may stand in a signed charging-only space (an electric vehicle may stay up to 30 minutes after disconnecting) applies on public highways and private roads open to public traffic, and in a parking lot only where the city, town or village has adopted it, so in your own lot set the rule in the lease.

title: No Eviction Fees or Penalties in a New York Lease
bodyText: A New York lease cannot charge a tenant a fee or penalty for being evicted or taken to court. You may not assess any fee, surcharge or other charge for legal services, which includes court fees, attorney fees, notary charges and administrative fees, unless a court orders it, and any lease term to the contrary is void. In an eviction case you may seek only the rent itself, whatever the lease says. Attorney fees are for the court to award: if your lease lets you recover them, the tenant gets the same right against you, and you cannot recover them on a default judgment. The library offers no eviction-fee clause.

title: A Lease Cannot Name Someone to Accept Eviction Papers
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution lets a lease name a person to accept eviction papers for the tenant. The notice of petition and petition, and the 14-day rent demand, must be served in one of the ways the eviction statute lists: by handing them to the tenant; by leaving them with a person of suitable age and discretion who lives or works at the property; or, if neither can be done, by posting them on a conspicuous part of the property or sliding them under the entrance door. Leaving them with another person, or posting or sliding them, must be followed within one day by mailing them to the tenant by both certified or registered mail and regular first-class mail. Any adult who is not a party may serve the papers. A lease clause naming a service agent would not replace these steps, so the library does not offer one. If the tenant is in New York's address confidentiality program, the Secretary of State is the tenant's agent for service of process and service is complete when the Secretary receives the papers.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure or Fee
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution sets up an expedited deposit disposition on the tenant's request, or a fee for one. The rule is already short: the itemized statement and the balance are due within 14 days after the tenant vacates. You may return the deposit sooner, but do not charge for it: a fee is not one of the four things you may keep from the deposit, and for an interest-bearing account the law lets you keep only a one-percent-a-year administration sum 'in lieu of all other administrative and custodial expenses'. Rent-controlled units, some senior-care facilities and rent-stabilized units follow their own deposit rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: No Statutory Absence Notice
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, or requires a lease to say anything about one, so the duty exists only if your lease creates it. If you want notice, use the optional clause `extended-absence-notice-ny`, which has the tenant give written notice and contact details before a long absence and makes the tenant responsible for damage the notice would have let you prevent. An absence alone does not end the tenancy or let you treat the home as abandoned: you may enter only as the lease and law allow (`edu-landlord-entry-ny`), and removing belongings or changing the locks while the tenant still has the right to possession is unlawful eviction (`edu-unlawful-eviction-ny`). If you believe a tenant has truly left for good, follow `edu-abandoned-property-ny` and `edu-mitigation-ny`.

title: Child Care in a Rented Home
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to let a tenant run a family day care home or other child care business in a rented home, or limits the conditions you may set, so the residential-use clause in your lease bars it unless you agree otherwise. If you want to allow it, use `family-child-care-consent-ny`, which requires the tenant to hold the state registration or license, comply with zoning and building codes, carry liability insurance, and keep within a set number of children. Under state law, a family day care home (generally three to six children, up to eight with school-age children) and small day care centers must register with the Office of Children and Family Services, and group family day care homes (seven to twelve children) and larger centers must be licensed. Do not ask parents to sign waivers releasing you from liability for your own negligence, because New York voids such waivers (`edu-exculpation-ny`). State law bars cities, towns, villages and counties from prohibiting or restricting registered or licensed family and group family day care in one- or two-family houses and multiple dwellings, or from imposing stricter health, fire or building standards because of it; that limit binds local governments, not landlords, so it does not stop your lease from forbidding child care.

title: Hunting, Fishing and Trapping on Rented Land
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution says whether a tenant of farmland or rural property gets hunting, fishing or trapping rights unless the owner grants them, so state it in the lease (`hunting-fishing-consent-ok`). New York's wildlife law treats a lessee or lawful occupant much like the owner: either may post the land against hunting, order an unpermitted hunter to leave, and let a guest shoot closer than 500 feet to the dwelling the lessee occupies, though never within 500 feet of anyone else's home, a school or another protected building. Resident lessees and their immediate families who actually occupy and farm the land may hunt (except deer and bear), trap and fish there without a license. An owner, lessee or occupant generally owes no duty to keep the land safe for people who come to hunt or fish, with exceptions such as willful or malicious failure to warn and entry for a fee.

title: No Fee-in-Lieu-of-Deposit Statute
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution sets up a fee, bond or insurance program in place of a security deposit, the way some states do. Without one, New York's general rules decide: you may not demand any fee before or at the beginning of the tenancy other than the capped screening fee, so a nonrefundable deposit-alternative fee collected at move-in is barred, and a sum held as security is a deposit that must be fully refundable under the deposit law. A recurring charge during the tenancy is not addressed by statute, but it is not rent you can claim in an eviction case. The library does not offer a fee-in-lieu clause; if you use a third-party deposit-replacement product, have it reviewed, because whether it is a lawful insurance or surety product is a question of the Insurance Law that the library does not answer.

title: Fees for Services You Do Not Provide
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution bars, in words, a residential landlord's charging a fee for a service it does not provide; the express rule (a charge 'for any service not actually rendered', with a triple-damages forfeiture) binds hotel, inn, motel and motor-court keepers, not landlords. Other rules come close. You may not charge any fee before or at the beginning of the tenancy except the capped screening fee, and no fee other than rent can be sought in an eviction case. A charge for a service you do not deliver can also be an unfair, deceptive or abusive practice under the consumer-protection law (`edu-consumer-protection-ny`). Charge only for services you actually provide and describe in the lease.

title: New York's Fire and Building Code
bodyText: Outside New York City, rental buildings are governed by the New York State Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code, which a state council adopts and amends and which covers construction, the condition and maintenance of existing buildings, and fire safety. Every city, town and village must enforce it (or leave enforcement to the county), and the Uniform Code overrides conflicting local building rules, though New York City keeps its own building and fire codes. The code is in Department of State regulations (19 NYCRR Parts 1219-1229). It adopts by reference the 2020 Residential, Building, Plumbing, Mechanical, Fuel Gas, Fire, Property Maintenance and Existing Building Codes of New York State, published by the International Code Council, with New York changes. The Residential Code governs detached one-family homes, detached two-family homes in which each unit has its own means of egress, and townhouses, each up to three stories above grade (the Building Code may be used for them instead), and the Building Code other buildings; the Fire Code reaches all buildings and premises, new or existing, and how they are used and occupied; and the Property Maintenance Code reaches all existing buildings and premises and their occupancy. The text of those model codes is a separate publication these rows do not hold, so their specific rules are not stated here. Local code officials must inspect multiple dwellings for fire safety and property maintenance at least every three years (`edu-rental-inspection-ny`). An order to remedy a code violation must be served within five days of its date and fully complied with within 30 days of its date, and it may require you to start at once or take protective steps meanwhile; failing to comply, or knowingly violating the code, can bring a fine of up to $1,000 a day or jail. Where the Multiple Dwelling Law or Multiple Residence Law applies, its own fire-escape and egress rules apply as well (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Fire Sprinkler Requirements
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to retrofit an existing apartment building or rental house with a full sprinkler system, and none imposes a separate high-rise sprinkler rule. Where the Multiple Dwelling Law or Multiple Residence Law applies, some older buildings must have sprinkler heads in particular spaces (certain hotels and rooming houses, cellars, public halls and stairs) or may use them in place of fire-retarding or a second exit, and the housing department may order them in existing buildings where a second exit is impractical. Outside New York City, sprinklers for new construction and alterations are set by the model codes the state Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code adopts by reference (the 2020 Building, Residential and Existing Building Codes of New York State), and the Fire Code it adopts reaches existing buildings too; these rows do not hold those codes' text, so whether they require sprinklers in a given building is not stated here. For new one- and two-family homes state law has made sprinklers a buyer's option rather than a requirement. Whatever the building has, every lease must say in bold whether there is a maintained and operative sprinkler system and, if so, when it was last maintained and inspected (`sprinkler-disclosure-ny`). New York City's sprinkler rules are local law.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to tell a prospective or new tenant that the property is in foreclosure, even after you have been served with a foreclosure complaint; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The notice duty falls on the foreclosing lender instead, which must give each tenant a bold, colored-paper notice within 10 days of serving the summons and complaint, and tenants then have the post-foreclosure rights in `edu-foreclosure-ny`. If you want to record that you told the tenant, the optional `foreclosure-disclosure-nv` clause does so. Never misstate a pending foreclosure if a prospective tenant asks.

title: Redeeming a Long Lease After Eviction
bodyText: New York's statutory right to redeem a lease after an eviction applies only to a nonpayment eviction where more than five years of the lease term remain when the warrant issues. In that case the tenant (or the tenant's executor, administrator or assignee, and in some cases a judgment creditor or mortgagee of the lease) may, within one year after the warrant is executed, pay all rent in arrears with interest and your costs and charges, and get the premises back under the original lease, subject to any new lease you signed in the meantime until the next May 1. A lease may waive this right in its terms. Ordinary residential leases of one or two years never qualify, so the library adds no clause; before the warrant is executed, the tenant's right to pay and stay is in `edu-redemption-ny`.

title: No Frozen Code Edition in Housing Law
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution writes a fixed edition of a model building, fire or property maintenance code into the warranty of habitability or into landlord-tenant law. The state's Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code is a regulation that a state council adopts and amends from time to time, generally effective at least 90 days after notice in the State Register, so the version that applies is the one in force when the work is done or the condition is judged. That regulation does name dated editions: outside New York City it currently adopts the 2020 editions of the New York State versions of the International Code Council's model codes (publication date November 2019), including the 2020 Property Maintenance Code of New York State for existing buildings, and those editions stay in force until the council amends the regulation. These rows do not hold the model codes' text. A few statutes name a dated standard for one item, such as the 2003 ASTM standard for pool safety covers, but none for rental housing generally. The warranty of habitability is a general standard of fitness and safety, not a code edition (`edu-habitability-ny`).

title: Renting Furnished
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution sets special rules for a furnished rental, so list the furniture and its condition in the lease (`furnishings-included-la`). Renting furnished does not raise the deposit limit: all deposits and advances together may not exceed one month's rent, and you may keep part of it only for damage beyond normal wear and tear and the other listed costs. Offer the tenant the move-in inspection the deposit law requires and note the furniture's condition in the signed agreement, because you cannot later deduct for any defect that agreement records. Rooms rented for single room occupancy in a multiple dwelling in New York City, another city of 325,000 or more or a locality whose adoption of the Multiple Dwelling Law takes in that rule carry their own cleaning rules for furniture and bedding.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText: New York has no statute on residential lease guaranties beyond the rule that a promise to pay another person's debt must be in writing and signed by the guarantor, so whether a guarantor stays liable after the lease is renewed, extended, continued month to month or changed depends on what the guaranty says and on case law. State it plainly: the optional guaranty clause (`guaranty-as`) has the guarantor sign the lease, sets a maximum, and makes you choose whether it covers renewals and continuations. You may not collect a deposit, prepayment or fee from a guarantor beyond what you could collect from the tenant: New York's one-month cap on deposits and advances and its ban on move-in payments other than rent, the deposit and screening fees are not limited to money paid by the tenant. A guarantor's written consent must accompany a tenant's request to sublet in a building of four or more units and an estate's request to assign or end a deceased tenant's lease. Requiring a guarantor only from applicants with housing vouchers or other lawful income could be source-of-income discrimination (`edu-fair-housing-ny`).

title: No Guest Day Limit in New York Leases
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution defines a guest or caps how long a guest may stay, so New York leases in this library use `guest-policy-ny`, which allows reasonable, temporary guest stays without a day count. The common clause limiting guests to 14 days unless you consent to add them is not offered for New York, because a guest who begins living in the unit becomes an occupant, and New York lets a tenant on a one-tenant lease who (or whose spouse) lives there as a primary residence add one occupant (and that occupant's dependent children) without your consent; on a lease with several tenants, occupants may replace departing tenants up to the number of tenants named, as long as at least one tenant (or a tenant's spouse) lives there as a primary residence, again without your consent. What you may require is that the tenant tell you the occupant's name within 30 days after the person moves in or within 30 days after you ask, and you may limit occupancy to meet federal, state or local occupancy laws (`permitted-occupants-ny`). A lease term waiving these rules is void, and a tenant can sue for an injunction and damages. Short-term rentals of the unit to paying guests are a separate subject (`edu-short-term-rental-ny`).

title: No Separate Statutory Guest Rights
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant's guests or suppliers their own rights of access, sets special guest rules for buildings of three or more households, or addresses guest fees. New York's rules on guests run through the tenant: the tenant is liable for housing-law violations caused by a guest's wilful act or negligence, and the retaliation protections do not apply where a guest caused the condition complained of. The real limit is the occupancy law: a guest who moves in becomes an occupant, whom a tenant may add within the limits of `permitted-occupants-ny` without your consent and without a fee, and any lease term restricting that is unenforceable (`edu-guest-day-limit-ny`). No statute bars a charge for a temporary guest, but charging to let the tenant have the occupant the law allows would restrict occupancy, and no fee other than rent can be collected in an eviction case, so the library offers no guest fee. Your rules for guests' use of the building must be reasonable and applied alike to everyone (`guest-policy-ny`, `rules-ny`).

title: No Materiality Threshold for Habitability in New York
bodyText: New York's warranty of habitability sets no materiality threshold. The statute states the standard (the home and common areas fit for human habitation and the uses the parties intended, with no condition dangerous, hazardous or detrimental to life, health or safety) without saying how serious a defect must be, and a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found no habitability materiality rule. Seriousness matters to the remedy instead. A court may stay a nonpayment case only for a condition that constructively evicts the tenant from part of the home or is, or is likely to become, dangerous to life, health or safety. The court rent deposit proceedings need a lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, another dangerous condition that has lasted five days, or rodent infestation. How courts weigh minor defects in damages is case law, which was not searched, so treat every reported defect as one you must fix.

title: No Part of the Warranty of Habitability Can Be Modified
bodyText: No part of New York's warranty of habitability can be changed by the lease: the statute voids an agreement modifying the tenant's rights as well as one waiving them, and it names no duty a lease may drop. So a lease cannot waive the water or hot-water supply where the home has no well or utility connection, as some states allow. The warranty adjusts itself in two places only. A condition caused by the misconduct of the tenant or persons under the tenant's direction or control is not a breach. And a court excludes damages for a breach caused by a strike or labor dispute not caused primarily by you (except to the extent of your net savings), if you tried in good faith to cure it where practicable. In a multiple dwelling you also stay responsible for keeping the building in good repair, while the tenant is liable too for a violation the tenant, the household or a guest causes by a wilful act or negligence.

title: Habitability Presumptions and Burdens in New York
bodyText: No New York statute presumes that you breached the warranty of habitability or that you took too long to repair; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. Three rules shift the proof, though. If a housing agency has issued a notice or order to repair and the tenant asks the court to stay a nonpayment case, you bear the burden of disproving the condition as the notice or order describes it. In New York City, the agency violation notices and orders kept by the central violations bureau are prima facie evidence of what they state. And if, within a year after a tenant's good-faith repair or code complaint or action to enforce the warranty, you serve a notice to quit, start an eviction or try to substantially change the tenancy, retaliation is presumed and you must prove another motive (except in owner-occupied buildings with fewer than four units, and where the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the condition).

title: No Habitability Statement Required in a New York Lease
bodyText: No New York statute makes you write a habitability promise into a residential lease; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. You do not need one, because the law puts the warranty into every written or oral residential lease: you are deemed to promise that the home and common areas are fit for human habitation and free of conditions dangerous to life, health or safety. Adding your own wording gains you nothing, and wording that promises less is void. The library's maintenance clause states your repair commitment in plain terms without narrowing the warranty. Manufactured home park rent-to-own contracts are different: they must state that the park owner is responsible for the warranty, and they are outside these rows.

title: No Habitability Waiver in a New York Lease
bodyText: You cannot use a New York lease, rider, renewal or house rule to waive or water down the warranty of habitability: any agreement by a tenant waiving or modifying it is void. The statute has no exception for a rent reduction or a separate signed document, so a clause in which the tenant accepts the unit as is, or accepts named defects in exchange for lower rent, is void too. The only adjustment is the statute's own: a condition caused by the misconduct of the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction or control is not a breach. The heating-fuel offset in multiple dwellings and the court rent deposit proceedings carry their own non-waiver sentences. Whether a tenant may release a claim that has already arisen is a question for case law, which the library did not search, so if you settle a dispute, use a stand-alone release signed after the fact, limited to that claim, and take advice. Market-rate rules only: regulated units follow their own rules.

title: Contamination and Environmental Easement Notices
bodyText: New York has two contamination rules that reach leases. First, if a party cleaning up a site under a state order or agreement, or the Department of Environmental Conservation, gives you indoor air test results for your property that exceed Health Department or OSHA indoor air guidelines, you must give every tenant and occupant the Health Department fact sheet and timely notice of any required public meeting, and the test results and any closure letter on request, within 15 days; and where an engineering control (such as a sub-slab ventilation system) is in place to mitigate indoor air contamination, or the property is under ongoing monitoring in a remedial program, you must give each prospective tenant the fact sheet before the lease is signed and put a prescribed notice in bold, at least 12-point type, on the first page of the lease (`indoor-air-test-notice-ny`). Second, property subject to an environmental easement held by the Department carries the owner's agreement to incorporate the easement in any lease of the affected area, the easement binds lessees, and because deeds and later instruments of conveyance must state in bold, at least 15-point type that the property is subject to the easement (and whether a lease counts is unsettled), the lease clause carries that statement too (`environmental-easement-ny`). No section of the Consolidated Laws requires a general disclosure of past contamination to tenants otherwise; sellers have separate disclosure forms. Lead paint and lead-safe certification are covered elsewhere (`edu-lead-ny`, `edu-lead-safe-certification-ny`).

title: No Duty to Supply Health Rules
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to give tenants a copy of health department rental rules on request or to refer them to a health district; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The State Sanitary Code applies statewide, counties, cities, towns and villages may add their own sanitary regulations, and local boards of health enforce both; any local rule on rentals is local law these rows do not research.

title: Renting Out a Condominium, Co-op or HOA Home
bodyText: Your tenant must follow the association's rules through the lease (`hoa-compliance`), and as the unit owner you remain bound by the by-laws, which may restrict or set conditions on leasing (for example a board approval requirement). If you own a condominium unit you do not live in and fall more than 60 days behind on common charges after any grace period, the board must give written notice telling your tenant to pay the rent to the condominium association until you are current (where a majority of the board was elected by and from among owners who live in their units, the board may choose not to); the tenant's payment to the association then counts against your rent and is a complete defense to your nonpayment case. New York sets no cap on association approval fees and no rule on association-held tenant deposits, but you may not pass an application, approval or move-in fee to the tenant at or before the start of the tenancy, and any deposit you hold is capped at one month's rent (`edu-application-fee-ny`, `edu-deposit-rules-ny`); co-op boards may charge processing fees only to buyers who become shareholders. No statute decides whether a later-adopted leasing restriction binds you or limits the tenant information an association may demand; that is for the governing documents and case law. Child care, display and other tenant rights against associations are covered in their own rows (`edu-no-family-child-care-rule-ny`, `edu-no-display-rule-ny`).

title: Home Businesses in a Rented Home
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented home as against the landlord, or limits what a lease may say about one, so your lease's residential-use clause (`residential-use-only`) bars business use unless you agree otherwise. If you want to allow a particular business, use the optional permission clause (`home-business-permission-co`), which keeps the home mainly a residence and requires the tenant to hold any required licences and permits, carry insurance and avoid disturbing neighbours. A lease is void, and you may re-enter, if the tenant uses the premises for an illegal trade, manufacture or other business, and you can be liable if you knowingly allow it (`edu-illegal-use-eviction-ny`). Child care has its own state registration and licensing rules (`edu-no-family-child-care-rule-ny`). Local zoning rules on home occupations are named, not researched.

title: No Homestead or Exemption Waiver in a New York Lease
bodyText: A homestead-waiver clause has no work to do in a New York residential lease. New York's homestead exemption protects a home the debtor owns and lives in (land with a dwelling, cooperative shares, a condominium unit or a mobile home), not a tenant's leasehold, so a tenant's waiver of it is empty rather than lawful. A lease term pledging a tenant's legally exempt belongings as security for rent is void, and a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found no section letting a lease waive any exemption from collection. Several exemptions, such as unemployment and workers' compensation benefits, say expressly that they cannot be waived. Collect unpaid rent through the court, subject to the tenant's exemptions.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Violations
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about outstanding housing code violations, inspection reports, vacate orders or condemnation proceedings, and the manufactured home park law has no condemnation-notice rule; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The nearest state rule is the certificate of occupancy notice: an owner of a property with three or fewer rental units must say in bold type, before the lease is signed, whether a required certificate of occupancy is currently valid (`certificate-of-occupancy-notice-ny`). Violations still matter: they can support a tenant's habitability claim and, in cities of 400,000 or more, a rent-impairing violation left on the city's records for more than six months after notice can bar you from recovering rent for the affected unit while it stays uncorrected. New York City and other localities keep public violation records and may add disclosure rules; these rows name local law but do not research it. Never misstate a known condition if a prospective tenant asks.

title: Penalty for Skipping the Inspection Offers
bodyText: New York's deposit law sets no separate forfeiture for failing to offer the move-in inspection or to send the written notice of the pre-move-out inspection right. The general remedy covers it: a landlord who violates any of the deposit rules is liable for the tenant's actual damages, and one who does so willfully can owe punitive damages of up to twice the deposit. In practice a missed offer also weakens your proof, because you bear the burden of showing that what you kept was reasonable, and the signed move-in agreement and pre-move-out statement are the evidence the law contemplates. Forfeiture of the whole deposit applies to missing the 14-day itemized statement (`edu-deposit-penalty-ny`). See `edu-move-in-inspection-ny`.

title: Key Control and Staff Screening
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to keep a written key-control policy or to run background checks on employees or contractors who have keys or codes to apartments, at any size of building. A sound practice is still worth having: log who holds master keys and codes, collect them when staff leave, re-key or reset after a loss, and enter only as the lease and the law allow (`edu-landlord-entry-ny`). In a multiple dwelling in New York City, another city of 325,000 or more or a locality that has adopted the Multiple Dwelling Law, with 13 or more families where you do not live, a janitor, housekeeper or other person responsible for you must live in the building or within 200 feet. If you screen employees for criminal history, New York employment law limits how a conviction may be used; these rows do not cover it.

title: What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: A tenant's main remedies when you fail to keep the home habitable are in `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ny`: damages or rent abatement under the warranty of habitability, a court stay of a nonpayment case, a court order to repair, and court rent deposit proceedings. Three statutes go further and stop rent itself. In a multiple dwelling, a rent-impairing violation (a fire hazard or serious threat to life, health or safety on the agency's list) left uncorrected six months after the agency's notice bars rent for the affected unit while it lasts, if the tenant deposits the rent with the court; this applies in cities of 400,000 or more under the Multiple Dwelling Law and elsewhere under the Multiple Residence Law, but not where the tenant, the household, guests or another resident caused the violation or the tenant refused you entry to fix it. Where a public welfare official pays a tenant's rent, the official may withhold it while a reported violation dangerous to life or health is outstanding, and you cannot evict or win a money judgment for that period.
