And no rent can be recovered while a multiple dwelling is occupied without a required certificate of occupancy (`edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-ny`).

title: Landlord Liability Insurance
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to show proof of it to tenants or a municipality, or to state its coverage in the lease. Carrying it is still prudent, because a lease cannot shift liability for your own negligence to the tenant: any lease term exempting you from liability for injuries caused by your or your staff's negligence in operating or maintaining the property is void (`edu-exculpation-ny`). Tell tenants your insurance does not cover their belongings (`tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca`), and every lease must carry the flood notice that encourages renters to check their own coverage (`flood-disclosure-ny`). Some cities and towns require insurance as part of rental registration; those local laws are not covered here.

title: Your Remedies When a New York Tenant Defaults
bodyText: You can take back a rented home only through a summary proceeding in court (`edu-eviction-process-ny`); in it you may also ask for a judgment for the rent due and, for a period when no rent is due, the fair value of use and occupancy, but no late fees or other charges. Other money the tenant owes, such as damage beyond normal wear and tear or rent for the rest of the term after the tenant leaves early, is claimed in a separate lawsuit, and you must try to re-rent the unit and prove your loss (`edu-mitigation-ny`); a claim for rent alone, without possession, is also an ordinary lawsuit for money. Which court hears a money claim depends on its size: New York City Civil Court up to $50,000, city and district courts up to $15,000, town and village justice courts up to $3,000, county courts up to $25,000, and the Supreme Court any amount. Small claims parts hear claims up to $10,000 in New York City, $5,000 in city and district courts and $3,000 in justice courts, but a corporation, partnership or association may not sue there. A business landlord with its principal office in New York uses the commercial claims part of the New York City Civil Court or a city or district court instead, limited to five claims a month; for a claim against a tenant, treat the lease as a consumer transaction and mail the court's demand-letter form 10 to 180 days before filing. Attorney's fees need a court order, and a landlord gets none on a default judgment (`edu-attorney-fees-ny`).

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText: New York caps late fees for every residential dwelling unit: no late fee until rent is more than five days late, and then no more than $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less. A lease term allowing more is void, and a late fee cannot be claimed in an eviction case. The library's late-fee clause (`late-fee`) is built within these caps; the full rule and the separate five-day certified-mail notice are in `edu-late-fee-ny`. Manufactured home parks (outside these rows) have their own late-charge limit, and cooperative shareholders paying maintenance under a proprietary lease follow a separate cooperative rule.

title: Police Cooperation and Crime-Free Leases
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires or regulates crime-free lease addenda, or requires you to cooperate with police by reporting on or giving information about tenants, with one exception: in an emergency affecting a multiple dwelling or multiple residence (fire, gas leak, collapse, natural disaster, terrorism and the like), you must give police, fire and other emergency personnel who ask the names and contact information of affected residents as listed in the lease (`emergency-contact-consent-ny`). What New York does regulate is the other direction: a tenant or occupant may call for police or emergency help without any penalty, and a lease term limiting that right is void (`edu-emergency-assistance-ny`). Illegal use of the premises voids the lease and is a removal ground, and you may act on lease breaches and illegal activity unrelated to the call (`edu-purpose-limitation-ny`, `criminal-activity-ny`). The state Constitution protects homes against unreasonable searches, and whether you may let police into a rented home without the tenant's consent or a warrant turns on case law, so get legal advice before giving police a key or access. Local crime-free housing ordinances are named, not researched.

title: Lead Rental Registry and Certification
bodyText: Outside New York City, state law has the Health Department build a rental registry of residential buildings with two or more units built before 1980 that are in communities the Department has named as communities of concern, and the owners of those buildings must have them inspected and certify them as free of lead paint hazards, filing the certification with the local health department by October 1 of the year it is due. The Department's regulations set the schedule (at least every three years), the inspection standards and who may inspect, and the inspection must at least include a visual check for deteriorated paint and soil and dust wipe samples. The Department must notify you if your building qualifies and send at least two reminders before the deadline, and failing to file, or filing a false certification, carries civil penalties. New York does not require the certification to be attached to the lease or given to the tenant. The law is set to be repealed on November 3, 2028, and these rows have not read the Department's regulations, so follow the notices you receive. The federal disclosure still applies to every pre-1978 rental (`lead-based-paint`), and New York City's lead law (Local Law 1 of 2004) is local law these rows name but do not research.

title: No State Lead Notices With the Lease
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for housing built before 1978 (`lead-based-paint`), New York State law requires no lead notice, certificate or packet to be given with a lease; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. State lead law works through the Health Department instead: it can order a lead paint condition corrected in a high-risk area (and a tenant's moving out does not end that duty), and outside New York City it requires certain pre-1980 buildings to be registered and certified free of lead paint hazards (`edu-lead-safe-certification-ny`). New York City's Local Law 1 of 2004 and other local lead laws have their own notices and annual inquiries; these rows name them but do not research them.

title: No Initials Required in a Lease
bodyText: No New York statute requires a tenant to initial, or separately sign, any clause of a residential lease, or makes a lease term enforceable only if initialed; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The tenant's signature on the lease is what binds the tenant. What New York does regulate is format: the sprinkler notice and, for owners of three or fewer rental units, the certificate of occupancy notice must be in bold, and the whole lease must meet the type-size and plain-language rules (`edu-small-print-ny`, `edu-plain-language-ny`). The Good Cause Eviction Law notice must be included in every initial and renewal lease, but it has no signature or initials line (`good-cause-notice-ny`). Asking for initials beside the rent, term, late fee and any automatic renewal is still good practice, because it helps show the tenant saw those terms.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: New York never requires you to record or register a residential lease, and recording one does not change any landlord-tenant right. A lease for three years or less is outside the recording law altogether. A lease for more than three years may be recorded with the county clerk (or the register, in counties that have one), or you may record a shorter memorandum of lease signed by all parties and acknowledged; an unrecorded lease of more than three years is void against a later good-faith buyer for value who records first. Once a lease or memorandum is recorded, an unrecorded agreement modifying it is void against a later good-faith buyer, and the tenant's possession is not notice of the modification. New York has no special rule for leases to the owner's relatives. Whether a tenant's possession alone warns a buyer or lender of an unrecorded long lease is a question for case law, which these rows did not research, so record a memorandum when a lease runs more than three years.

title: Long Leases: Writing, Recording and Term Limits
bodyText: New York sets no maximum term for an ordinary residential lease and does not require a seal, a spouse's signature or consent, or any special formality beyond these: a lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed by you or an agent authorized in writing (`edu-statute-of-frauds-ny`). A lease for more than three years counts as a conveyance under the recording law, so if it is not recorded (or a memorandum of it is not recorded, signed and acknowledged by all parties) it is void against a later good-faith buyer or lender who records first; tenants on long leases may ask to record a memorandum. Two kinds of owner face limits: a life tenant (someone who owns the property only for life) can lease for no more than 21 years, and a longer lease is void as to the excess, though the tenant's rights may end sooner, when the life estate ends (`edu-life-tenant-lessor-ny`); and a religious corporation needs leave of a court or the attorney general to lease its real property for more than five years. If you own the property jointly with a spouse or anyone else, who must sign turns on your deed and case law, so have every owner sign a long lease.

title: No Parity Rule Between Lease Types
bodyText: No New York statute stops you from offering a month-to-month tenancy on different terms or at a different rent from a fixed-term lease, or caps the difference; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The general rules still apply to both: the fee and deposit limits, the notice you must give before a non-renewal or a rent increase of 5% or more (`edu-rent-increase-notice-ny`), and, where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, its presumption against increases above the local rent standard (`edu-rent-control-ny`). If you accept rent after a lease of more than a month ends, the tenancy becomes month to month unless you agree otherwise (`edu-holdover-ny`). Price differences must never track a protected class (`edu-fair-housing-ny`). Rent-stabilized tenants choose between one- and two-year renewals under their own rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Deadlines for Suing a Tenant
bodyText: A suit on the lease, such as for unpaid rent or other money the lease makes the tenant owe, must be started within six years; a suit for damage to the property as an injury to property, or to enforce a liability created by statute, within three years. A claim arising from a consumer credit transaction must be brought within three years, and once that period ends no later payment or acknowledgment revives it; no statute says whether unpaid rent is such a claim, and the library did not search case law, so the cautious course is to sue within three years. Otherwise, to restart a period that has run, you need an acknowledgment or new promise in a writing the tenant signs, though a payment may also have effect. No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York sets a shorter limit for rent claims in an eviction case. Rent-regulated overcharge claims follow their own rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Liquidated Damages in a Lease
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution allows or limits an agreed damages amount in a residential lease; the statutory liquidated-damages rules are for sales and leases of goods. Whether a fixed sum is an enforceable estimate or a void penalty is decided by case law, which the library has not read, so expect a figure far above your likely loss to be challenged. Several statutes already fix the outcome: the deposit is refundable except for the listed actual costs, so it cannot be kept as liquidated damages; late fees are capped; a tenant who vacates early must be credited with your duty to re-rent, which a lease cannot waive; and legal or administrative fees need a court order. For leaving early, use an early-termination option (`edu-no-early-termination-fee-rule-ny`) rather than a damages formula; holdover rates are in `edu-holdover-rate-ny`.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: New York has no lockout option for unpaid rent, and a lease clause allowing one is unlawful to use. A tenant or lawful occupant may be removed only through a court proceeding and a warrant executed by a sheriff, marshal or constable. Changing the lock without giving the occupant a key, plugging or disabling it, removing the door or belongings, or cutting off essential services to make an occupant leave is an unlawful eviction where the occupant has lived there 30 consecutive days or more or has a lease: it is a class A misdemeanor, carries a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation plus up to $100 a day, for no more than six months, from the occupant's request to be restored until you restore the occupant, and an occupant put out unlawfully can sue for treble damages. For unpaid rent, use the 14-day rent demand and a nonpayment proceeding (`edu-rent-demand-ny`, `edu-eviction-process-ny`). Full rules: `edu-unlawful-eviction-ny`.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to a New York Tenant
bodyText: New York has no statute that lets you shift your habitability or repair duties to a tenant, and the warranty of habitability cannot be waived or modified, so that duty always stays with you. What you can do is agree in the lease that the tenant will do specific chores, such as yard care or clearing snow from areas only the tenant uses; New York has no statute requiring a separate document for this, so the library's chore clauses bind as ordinary lease terms. In a multiple dwelling you stay responsible for keeping the building, lot and common parts in repair and clean (under the Multiple Dwelling Law in cities of 325,000 or more and places that adopt it, and the Multiple Residence Law elsewhere) and, under the Multiple Dwelling Law, for arranging daily removal of waste, even if a tenant agrees to help; the tenant is answerable for conditions the tenant, the household or guests cause. If a tenant skips an agreed chore, you have a claim against the tenant, but it is no defence to a habitability claim, so check the work gets done. A lease term making the tenant pay for repairs that are your duty, such as a per-repair deductible, risks being void as a modification of the warranty.

title: On-Bill Energy Efficiency Charges
bodyText: New York's on-bill energy efficiency charge is the Green Jobs-Green New York on-bill recovery charge: an owner who holds the meter account can finance energy efficiency work through the state energy authority and repay it on the electric or gas bill. Unless paid off before a sale or transfer, the charge stays with the meter when ownership, tenancy or the account holder changes, so a tenant who later holds the account can be billed for it; past-due charges at account closure stay with the customer who ran them up. The charge is treated like utility service for shutoff purposes, with the usual protections, but tenants who take over payments to keep service on in a multiple dwelling or two-family house are never billed for it. No statute requires you to tell a tenant about the charge (a seller must tell a buyer), but say so in the lease and decide who pays (`gjgny-charge-notice-ny`). A master meter carrying the charge cannot be converted to submetering.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: No New York statute requires a lease disclosure that the property is near a military air installation, in a noise or accident potential zone, or within a set distance of a military base, and none gives a tenant a right to end the lease on learning of it; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. New York's military statutes that touch leases protect service members instead, for example the right to end a lease on entering military service (`edu-servicemember-ny`). Local zoning around an installation may impose its own rules, which these rows do not research.

title: Renting to Minors and Naming Them in an Eviction
bodyText: In New York a minor is a person under 18. A lease signed by someone 18 or older cannot be disaffirmed for infancy, but no section of the Consolidated Laws of New York lets a person under 18 make a binding lease, so a minor's lease may be voidable; have an adult sign as tenant or guarantor. No statute bars naming a minor in an eviction case, but a minor appears in court through a parent, guardian or court-appointed guardian, and in an ordinary lawsuit papers for a minor go to the parent or guardian and, if the minor is 14 or older, to the minor too. Name the adults who signed the lease as respondents; for minors who only live in the home, ask the court or a lawyer how to name and serve them.

title: Unpaid Water and Sewer Charges as Liens
bodyText: In New York, unpaid municipal water rents and sewer rents are charged against the property served and become a lien on it, generally ahead of every other lien except taxes, whoever ran up the bill. State laws do this for village water rents, town water and sewer districts, sewer rents of cities, counties, towns and villages, second-class cities and several public authorities, and many cities have their own charter or local laws, which these rows do not research. No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York lets a lease clause, an affidavit filed with the water department, or the tenant's name on the account keep a tenant's unpaid water or sewer bill off your property. If the tenant pays the water or sewer provider directly, check the accounts regularly (`utility-payment-evidence`) and recover anything you pay for the tenant in an ordinary suit, or from the deposit if the lease makes that reimbursement payable to you (`utility-transfer-nj`); it is not rent (`edu-utility-submetering-ny`).

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits or Move-In Fees
bodyText: New York has no nonrefundable deposit, and no notice that can make part of a deposit nonrefundable. Every deposit or advance, whatever you call it (security, pet, cleaning, key or last month's rent), is capped with the others at one month's rent and is fully refundable when the tenant moves out, less only unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility charges the lease makes payable to you, and moving and storing the tenant's belongings. Calling the money a fee does not help: before or at the beginning of the tenancy you may collect only rent, the deposit or advance, and the capped background-and-credit-check fee. A lease term saying otherwise is void. See `edu-deposit-rules-ny`, `edu-pet-deposit-ny` and `due-at-signing-ny`.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Some states let a landlord keep part of a deposit as nonrefundable if a separate written notice says so. New York has no such notice, because it allows no nonrefundable deposit at all: every deposit or advance is refundable except for the four deductions the law lists, and a nonrefundable fee at move-in is barred. A separate notice, a signed acknowledgment or bold type does not change that. See `edu-nonrefundable-deposit-bar-ny`.

title: Out-of-State Owners: No Required New York Agent
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires an owner who lives outside New York to name a New York agent in the lease or before suing, and none requires a tenant to withhold tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. A nonresident who owns rental property in New York can be sued in New York courts on claims arising from it and served outside the state. In a Multiple Dwelling Law building the owner, any lessee of the whole building and the managing agent must register their names and addresses, and in New York City an unregistered owner cannot recover rent; New York City's registration rules are local law. A foreign corporation or LLC doing business in New York needs authority before it can sue (`edu-entity-landlord-court-ny`). Give tenants a current address for notices in any case (`edu-owner-identity-ny`).

title: No Fee for Serving Notices
bodyText: Do not charge a tenant for preparing or serving a rent demand, a notice of nonpayment, a termination notice or court papers. New York bars any fee for legal services connected with renting a residential unit unless a court orders it, and legal services include court fees, attorney fees, notary charges and administrative fees, including those for court proceedings. A lease term allowing a notice-service fee is void, and no fee other than rent can be sought in an eviction case. The library does not offer the clause. Any costs the law allows are for the court to award (`edu-attorney-fees-ny`).

title: Statutory Notices Cannot Be Waived in a New York Lease
bodyText: A New York lease cannot waive or shorten the notices the law requires before you end a tenancy or sue for rent: a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found no section allowing it. Those notices are the written 14-day rent demand before a nonpayment case, the 30, 60 or 90 days' written notice of non-renewal or of a renewal rent increase of 5% or more, the month-to-month termination notices, and the 30-day notice ending a tenancy at will or by sufferance. If you give the non-renewal or rent-increase notice late, the tenancy continues on its existing terms until the notice period runs out, whatever the lease says. A lease term waiving the court's hardship stay or the 30-day chance to cure a lease breach is void. A lease for a fixed term ends on its end date without notice, so nothing needs waiving there. The library offers no notice-waiver clause.

title: Extra Terms in a Move-Out Notice
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution regulates a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, or requires a warning when the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to the tenant's notice and the move-out date. Two statutes matter: a tenant who gives notice of intention to quit and then stays past that date owes double rent while in possession (`edu-holdover-ny`), so the date must be the tenant's own choice; and any added term must still fit New York's limits, so it cannot add fees, waive deposit or other rights that are void to waive, or charge legal fees without a court order (`edu-prohibited-terms-ny`). While a notice is pending you may not cut off essential services, change the locks or otherwise pressure the tenant to leave (`edu-unlawful-eviction-ny`).

title: Optional Lease Terms in New York
bodyText: The New York rows offer these optional clauses: building rules made part of the lease (`rules-ny`), landlord casualty termination (`casualty-termination-ny`), tenant-caused damage (`tenant-caused-damage-ny`), illegal use (`criminal-activity-ny`), automatic renewal (`auto-renewal-ny`), delivery of possession (`possession-delay`), a returned-payment fee and a late fee within the caps (`returned-payments-ny`, `late-fee`), and e-mail for routine communications (`electronic-notice-ny`). Some lawful options are declined, each with its reason in its own row: waiving the tenant's casualty exit (`edu-casualty-ny`), a holdover premium rate (`edu-holdover-rate-ny`), an agreement that rent accepted after expiry creates no month-to-month tenancy (`edu-holdover-ny`), an objectionable-tenant clause (`edu-nuisance-ny`), the seasonal deposit uplift (`edu-deposit-rules-ny`), a broader jury waiver (`edu-jury-waiver-ny`) and contractual interest (`edu-legal-interest-ny`); you may add your own clause for these. Legal or eviction fees without a court order and waivers of statutory protections are barred (`edu-prohibited-terms-ny`). If you add an option to purchase to a lease of a one- to four-family house (not a condominium or co-op unit), New York treats you as a seller: give the tenant the signed property condition disclosure statement before the lease-option is signed and attach a copy signed by both of you, because a willful failure makes you liable for the buyer's actual damages. New York has no general rent-to-own statute for houses (manufactured home park rent-to-own contracts and foreclosure sale-leasebacks have their own rules, outside these rows), so have a New York lawyer draft any purchase option.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meter Disclosures
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance site nearby or about a pending application to demolish the unit; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. Demolition does matter later: where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, a good-faith plan to demolish is a ground to end a tenancy only if you prove it by clear and convincing evidence (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`). Shared meters are regulated directly rather than by disclosure: if a tenant's gas, electric or steam meter also measures service outside the unit and the tenant pays for it, you must remove the shared meter, put those charges in your own name, or, only where the law allows, sign a written apportionment agreement with the tenant (`edu-utility-apportionment-ny`). That shared-meter rule cannot be waived.

title: Elevators, Garage Doors, Pools and Amenities
bodyText: A few New York statutes reach building facilities beyond the apartment itself. In a multiple dwelling, elevator shafts and doors must meet the safety rules of the Multiple Dwelling Law (New York City, other cities of 325,000 or more and localities that adopt it) or, elsewhere, in buildings erected on or after July 1, 1952, the Multiple Residence Law; under the Multiple Dwelling Law alone, a building erected after April 18, 1929 (outside New York City, after the date the law began to apply there) that is more than six stories or 60 feet high must have a passenger elevator operating at all times that reaches every apartment above the entrance story, and every self-service passenger elevator must have a mirror so a person can see inside before entering; only licensed elevator contractors and mechanics may work on or inspect elevators. An automatic garage door opener at a house or multiple dwelling must have an automatic-reverse and entrapment-protection feature, and anyone servicing one that fails must label it and notify you in writing. The state building code requires self-closing, self-latching, locked gates on pool enclosures and a pool alarm on any pool built or substantially modified after the rule took effect, and, outside New York City, its New York amendments require swimming pools to be completely enclosed by a permanent barrier unless the pool is a hot tub or spa with an approved safety cover (`edu-pool-safety-ny`). Tenants' groups may use a community or social room free of charge (`edu-tenant-organizing-ny`), and where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, separate charges for amenities such as a gym, parking or storage are not rent unless imposed to get around that law. Elevator inspection schedules and most other facility rules are in the model codes the state building code adopts by reference and in local codes, which these rows do not hold.

title: Ending a Lease Early to Move In (Not Offered)
bodyText: No New York statute gives you a right to end a fixed-term lease early because you or a relative want to move in; any such right would have to come from the lease, and the library does not offer that clause for New York. Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, you may remove a tenant only on a listed ground, and owner occupancy counts only if you prove by clear and convincing evidence a good-faith need for your own principal residence or a listed close relative's, no other suitable unit in the building is available, and the tenant is under 65 and not disabled; a lease clause cannot add a broader ground, and the tenancy's notice rules still apply (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-ny`). Elsewhere, whether a lease term ending the tenancy early for owner occupancy is enforceable is settled by case law, not statute. You may add your own clause after taking advice; either way, removing a tenant who stays still takes a court case.

title: Parking and Towing Rules
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to deliver parking rules before the lease is signed, prescribes a heading for them, limits the vehicle information you may ask for, or requires a waiting period before towing a tenant's car for expired registration or inspection. Attach your parking rules to the lease: under the library's rules clause (`rules-ny`), a new or changed rule binds the tenant during the term only if it is reasonable and the tenant accepts it in writing, and where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, only rules accepted in writing or made part of the lease at the start can support an eviction. Do not charge for a first parking permit or decal at the start of the tenancy (`parking-vehicle-rules-ny`). Outside New York City, a private parking lot with room for five or more vehicles must display a conspicuous notice naming the operator and the authorized tow or boot company and stating that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense, or no vehicle may be towed or booted from it, and you may not take any payment from the tow company. The tow company must notify the local police of each tow from private property (`edu-towing-ny`), and local towing laws, including New York City's, may add more.

title: No Article-Wide Non-Waiver Rule in New York
bodyText: New York has no counterpart to Colorado's rule making its whole habitability article non-waivable, and no non-waiver rule for a home sale-leaseback: a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found that New York writes its non-waiver rules section by section (the warranty of habitability, the duty to re-rent, the fee and deposit limits and others listed in `edu-prohibited-terms-ny`), with article-wide non-waiver sentences only for the court rent deposit proceedings.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives you a right to enter for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes or pest treatment, or sets notice or hours for those visits, so the right comes from the lease (`scheduled-services-entry-la`, `landlords-access`). List the services and their schedule, give notice before each visit, and keep visits to reasonable hours. Before a pesticide is applied inside or on the premises of a dwelling, the certified applicator must give the occupants the label information, including warnings; in a multiple dwelling the applicator gives it to you and you must make it available to occupants on request. In counties and cities that have opted into the state's lawn-application notice rules, owners of multiple family dwellings must pass the applicator's 48-hour advance notice on to occupants. New York City's Housing Maintenance Code has its own access rules, which these rows do not cover.

title: Pesticide Application Notices
bodyText: New York's pesticide notice rules run mainly through the certified applicator. Before applying a pesticide in or on a one- or two-family dwelling, the applicator must give the occupants the label information, including warnings, in the written, digital or electronic form they choose. In a building of three or more apartments, the applicator gives that information to you or your agent, and you must make it available to occupants on request at reasonable times; if a tenant hires an applicator for an apartment, the applicator gives it to the occupants. In a county or New York City that has adopted the state's lawn-pesticide neighbor notification law, the owner of a multiple-family dwelling must also pass the applicator's 48-hour written notice of a commercial lawn application to the occupants. No state statute requires a pest-control schedule notice in the lease; the Department of Environmental Conservation's pesticide rules (6 NYCRR) and local laws, which these rows do not cover, may add requirements.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to give a tenant a fact sheet or other notice about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat. The one statewide pet rule at eviction falls on the officer, not you: before executing a warrant, the sheriff or marshal must check for companion animals and arrange their care with the tenant, or with a humane society, SPCA or pound, and try to tell the tenant where the animals went (`edu-post-eviction-property-ny`). Your own pet rules are in `pet-policy-ny`. Local pet or animal-control rules are named, not researched.

title: Plain Language: No Waiver Statement or Readability Test
bodyText: New York's plain-language law applies to every written residential lease but asks only that it be clear and coherent, in words with everyday meanings, and divided into captioned sections (`edu-plain-language-ny`). It has no readability score, no required statement listing what the tenant could lose or waive, and no Attorney General preapproval; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The law does not apply to agreements involving more than $250,000, and it allows wording that a state or federal law requires, such as the Good Cause Eviction Law notice. A lease that falls short is not void and is no defense to its enforcement; the tenant can recover actual damages plus a $50 penalty (the penalties in all class actions over one lease form are capped at $10,000 in total; actual damages are not), a good-faith attempt to comply avoids the penalty, and no suit is allowed once both sides have fully performed.

title: Candidates, Canvassers and Tenant Civic Activity
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators a right to enter a private apartment building to canvass, or requires you to let them in, and none sets rules for political literature in lobbies or mailrooms. Tenants' own organizing is protected: you may not interfere with a tenant's right to form, join or take part in a tenants' group, or punish a tenant for doing so, and a tenants' group may meet without a fee in a community or social room or other common space, peaceably, at reasonable hours and without blocking access (`edu-tenant-organizing-ny`). Retaliating against a tenant for that activity is also barred (`edu-retaliation-ny`). Any building rule on solicitation or flyers should be applied the same way to every cause and every tenant. Flags and signs are covered in `edu-no-display-rule-ny`.

title: Swimming Pool Barriers and Alarms
bodyText: New York's pool safety rules for rental property come from the state Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code, which state law directs to require that any gate in a pool enclosure be self-closing and self-latching and be locked with a key, combination or other child-proof lock when the pool is not in use or supervised; that a residential pool built or substantially modified after the rule took effect have an alarm that detects a child entering the water (pools with a qualifying automatic power safety cover, and hot tubs or spas with a qualifying safety cover, are exempt); and that a temporary enclosure used while an in-ground pool is installed be replaced by a permanent one within 90 days of the local building permit or the start of installation, whichever is later (the local building department may extend that period). Outside New York City, the code's own New York amendments add that every swimming pool must be completely enclosed by a permanent barrier, except a hot tub or spa with a safety cover meeting the ASTM F1346 standard; the detailed barrier, fence and alarm specifications are in the 2020 Residential, Building and Property Maintenance Codes of New York State, which the Uniform Code adopts by reference and these rows do not hold. The Department of State posts a summary, and local laws may be stricter. No state statute requires a pool notice or pool rules in a lease. If you add pool rules, keep gates latched and barriers intact, avoid any term that excuses your own negligence (`edu-prohibited-terms-ny`), and take care that rules about children's use are justified by safety, since familial status is protected (`edu-fair-housing-ny`).

title: No Tenant Air Conditioner Right
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant in a market-rate unit a right to install a portable or window air conditioner, requires you to supply cooling, or sets a maximum indoor temperature for apartments. Whether a tenant may put in a window or through-the-wall unit is up to the lease (`portable-cooling-device-ia`, `no-alterations`), subject to a tenant's right to reasonable modifications and accommodations for a disability. In a building covered by the Multiple Dwelling Law or the Multiple Residence Law, access to a fire escape must not be obstructed in any way, so do not allow a unit in a window that opens onto a fire escape. Rent-regulated units follow their own rules, including a bar on surcharges for a tenant-installed air conditioner when the tenant pays for electricity (`edu-scope-ny`). New York City and other local codes may set cooling rules these rows do not cover.

title: No Tenant Solar Device Right
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant a right to install a plug-in, balcony or portable solar device, or limits your lease rules on solar equipment in a rental. Your alterations clause (`no-alterations`) and, if you want one, the optional solar clause (`portable-solar-mo`) decide, subject to a tenant's right to make reasonable modifications for a disability at the tenant's expense. New York's solar statute for homeowners' associations voids a deed, contract or other instrument that effectively prohibits a rooftop solar power system of up to 25 kilowatts; it is written for associations and does not say whether it reaches a lease, so if you rent a whole house, use consent with reasonable conditions rather than a flat ban on a rooftop system. Equipment connected to the utility grid must meet the utility's interconnection and safety standards.

title: Rules That Depend on Unit Counts
bodyText: Several New York rules turn on the number of units, counted in different ways, so check each one separately and read every exemption's conditions together (each requires all of its parts). Counted across your whole portfolio: where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, a small landlord (each natural owner holding no more than 10 units in the state, or the local law's number) is exempt, and must name its owners and their units in any eviction case to claim it (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`). Counted in the building or property: an owner-occupied building of 10 units or fewer is also outside the Good Cause law; a deposit for a property with six or more units must be held in an interest-bearing New York account (`edu-deposit-interest-ny`); a tenant in a building with four or more units has a right to sublet with your reasonable consent (`no-sublet-assign-ny`); an owner of three or fewer rental units must give the certificate of occupancy notice (`certificate-of-occupancy-notice-ny`); three or more households make a multiple dwelling; the retaliation law exempts only owner-occupied buildings with fewer than four units (`edu-retaliation-ny`); and the domestic violence, children and familial-status rules exempt only owner-occupied buildings of one or two units (`edu-fair-housing-ny`, `edu-children-occupancy-ny`). The federal Fair Housing Act's small-owner exemptions (no more than three single-family houses, or an owner-occupied building of up to four units) are broader than New York's, so they do not let you discriminate in New York. For buying rather than renting, an institutional investor (owning 10 or more one- or two-family homes, managing pooled investor funds, and holding $30 million or more) may not buy or offer on a one- or two-family home until it has been listed for sale to the public for 90 days. Mechanic's lien notice rules are not covered here; local laws with their own thresholds are named, not researched.

title: No Possession Bond in New York
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution provides for a bond, signed with the lease, in which the tenant agrees to deliver possession at the end of the term and confesses a judgment for possession. A confession of judgment in New York gives only a money judgment (`edu-confession-of-judgment-ny`), so removing a tenant who stays after the term still takes a summary proceeding in court (`edu-eviction-process-ny`).

title: Private Wells Serving Rentals
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to test a private well that serves a rental home or to give tenants the results. Whether your well becomes a regulated public water system, with testing, reporting and public-notice duties, depends on the State Sanitary Code (10 NYCRR Part 5), which these rows do not cover; state law uses the measure of a system serving at least five service connections used by year-round residents or regularly serving at least 25 year-round residents for its emerging-contaminant testing, which covered systems must do at least every three years, notifying property owners they serve of results at or above the state's notification levels. Well construction and repair standards are also set by Health Department rules, and local health departments may add their own. If tenants drink well water, testing it before each tenancy and sharing the results is a cautious practice, and you must keep the water supply adequate and the home habitable (`edu-habitability-ny`).

title: Acts the Tenant Must Not Do
bodyText: New York has no single statute listing acts a tenant must not commit, so the lease states them (`prohibited-acts-renter-pr`). The law does make a tenant answerable for damage the tenant causes: in a Multiple Dwelling Law or Multiple Residence Law building the tenant is liable for a violation caused by the tenant's own wilful act or negligence or that of a household member or guest, and a condition caused by the tenant's misconduct is not a breach of your warranty of habitability (`edu-tenant-duties-ny`). Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, you can evict for such acts only on one of its grounds, such as a substantial lease violation the tenant fails to cure within ten days of written notice, or a nuisance, or substantial damage done maliciously or through gross negligence (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`).

title: No Statute on Written Repair Promises in New York
bodyText: No New York statute requires a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date or to be made before the lease is signed; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. An unkept promise is still risky: it can be a breach of the lease, and a misleading promise in renting can be a deceptive business practice. If you promise work, list it with dates in the Promised Repairs section. A promise of work never reduces your duty to keep the home fit to live in.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: New York has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: no statute requires you to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, or to post exposure warnings in rental housing; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The warranty of habitability still bars conditions dangerous, hazardous or detrimental to tenants' health (`edu-habitability-ny`), and the federal lead disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing (`lead-based-paint`).

title: No Property-Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, or to certify rent paid for a tenant's tax credit; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. New York's real property tax circuit breaker credit lets an eligible renter treat 25% of adjusted rent as property tax, and the tenant figures it alone: adjusted rent leaves out heat, gas, electricity, furnishings and board, and if those are included in the rent but not separately stated in a written lease, the tenant must deduct a set percentage (15% to 50%). Stating any included utility or furnishing charges separately in the lease therefore helps a tenant claim the right amount. Rent increase exemptions for seniors and people with disabilities apply to rent-regulated units, which are outside these rows (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Unlawful Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: Yes: in New York, if a tenant or occupant uses the premises for any illegal trade, manufacture or other business, the lease becomes void and you may re-enter through a summary proceeding, and in a Multiple Dwelling Law building (cities of 325,000 or more and places that adopt that law) used as a house of prostitution with the tenant's permission you may end the lease at your election. You must still go to court to remove anyone, and where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, illegal use is a ground for removal (`edu-illegal-use-eviction-ny`, `criminal-activity-ny`). Knowingly leasing for, or permitting, an unlawful business makes you liable for resulting damage, and neighbors or public officials can force action. Your lease's residential-use clause (`residential-use-only`) covers lawful uses you do not want. A tenant may not be penalized under a local nuisance law for calling for police or emergency help (`edu-emergency-assistance-ny`).

title: Recycling: Local Rules Only
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, or to supply recycling containers; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. State law instead required every municipality to adopt, by September 1, 1992, a local law making people who leave solid waste for collection separate recyclables (paper, glass, metals, plastics, yard waste and any other materials with markets), so the separation rules, and any duty they put on building owners, come from the city, town or village. Your lease rules may require tenants to follow the local separation rules and tell them where the containers are (`rules-ny`). New York City and other localities have their own recycling and organics rules; these rows name local law but do not research it.

title: Paying Up to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: In a nonpayment case the tenant can stop the eviction by paying the full rent due. If the tenant pays it before the hearing, you must accept it and the case is moot; before the warrant issues, the tenant may also stay it by depositing the rent and court costs with the court; and after judgment, the court must vacate the warrant if the tenant tenders or deposits the full rent due at any time before it is executed, unless you show the rent was withheld in bad faith. These rights come from the eviction statute and a lease cannot shorten them. No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires special wording when you accept a partial payment, or says whether accepting one waives the nonpayment case; take advice before accepting part of the rent after you have started a case. See `edu-eviction-process-ny` and `edu-cure-ny`.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant a right to put a mezuzah or other religious or cultural item on the apartment door or doorframe, or limits your lease rules about such displays. Your display rule must still be written and applied the same way for every faith: New York's Human Rights Law makes it unlawful to discriminate because of creed in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental. A rule that bars a small religious item on a door while allowing other door decorations, or that is enforced only against one faith, invites a discrimination claim. The library's common-area rule (`common-area-use`) keeps any display the law entitles a tenant to make, and `edu-no-display-rule-ny` covers flags and signs. New York City and other local laws may add rules these rows do not cover.

title: When You Cannot Recover Rent
bodyText: New York bars recovering rent in a few building-law situations, all for multiple dwellings (under the Multiple Dwelling Law, a dwelling for three or more families living independently). First, for any period a multiple dwelling is occupied without the certificate of occupancy or compliance the Multiple Dwelling Law or Multiple Residence Law requires, you cannot recover rent or evict for nonpayment of it (`edu-certificate-of-occupancy-ny`). Second, where a rent-impairing violation (a fire hazard or serious threat to life, health or safety on the official list) stays uncorrected for six months after the department notifies you, you cannot recover rent for the affected apartments while it remains; the tenant must plead it and deposit the rent with the court, and the bar does not apply if the tenant caused the violation or refused you entry to fix it. This covers cities of 400,000 or more under the Multiple Dwelling Law and smaller cities, towns and villages under the Multiple Residence Law. Third, in New York City an owner who has not registered the multiple dwelling cannot recover rent until registering (`edu-sale-management-change-ny`). Outside the building laws, where the tenant receives public assistance, you cannot evict or get a money judgment for nonpayment for any period in which a violation dangerous to life or health, reported to the welfare department, was outstanding in the building (`edu-landlord-breach-remedy-ny`). Repair proceedings that redirect rent are in `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ny`.

title: Rent Increases During the Lease
bodyText: No New York statute governs a rent increase written into a market-rate lease, whether a fixed schedule or an index formula, or gives you a right to raise rent mid-term without one; during a fixed term the rent is what the lease says. Three state rules bear on it. Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, any increase that takes the rent up by more than the local rent standard in a calendar year is presumed unreasonable, and unpaid rent from an unreasonable increase is not good cause for eviction (`edu-rent-control-ny`). At renewal, an increase of 5% or more needs the advance written notice in `edu-rent-increase-notice-ny`. And under the retaliation law, attempting to substantially alter the terms of a tenancy within a year after a tenant's good-faith complaint is presumed retaliatory; New York has no safe harbor for increases the lease itself schedules, so keep scheduled increases fixed at signing rather than at your discretion. Rent-regulated units follow their own rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Rent Deposits and Counterclaims in Eviction Cases
bodyText: New York has no general rule that a tenant must pay rent into court before defending an eviction case or demanding a jury: the tenant may answer orally or in writing with any legal or equitable defense or counterclaim, and no section of the Consolidated Laws of New York makes a counterclaim compulsory. Deposits arise only in set cases. In New York City, after the tenant's second adjournment or 60 days after the first appearance, the court may, on your motion and weighing the equities, order the tenant to deposit rent or use and occupancy that falls due after the order, but not where the tenant shows certain defenses (such as hazardous violations, a colorable overcharge, an illegal unit or no personal jurisdiction), not above a regulated rent or the tenant's subsidy share, and not above 30% of a fixed income; if the tenant misses a deposit you may get an immediate trial, but the tenant's defenses are never dismissed for it. Elsewhere, and in New York City too, a tenant who wants the case stayed for a repair order or a dangerous condition, or who raises the rent-impairing violation defense in a multiple dwelling, must deposit the rent, and a tenant may stop a nonpayment warrant by depositing the rent due (`edu-redemption-ny`). The lease cannot add a deposit condition the statute does not impose.

title: Taking Rent Carries the Repair Duty
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution says in so many words, as the uniform act does, that a lease, assignment, deed or security instrument may not let someone receive rent free of the duty to maintain. New York gets close another way. The warranty of habitability is part of every residential lease and cannot be waived; whoever takes over the lease or the right to rent (a buyer, an assignee of the lease or of the rent) answers to the tenant for breaches of the lease just as the original landlord did; and outside New York City and Nassau and Suffolk Counties, a tenant's repair proceeding can be brought against anyone legally obliged to keep the unit habitable, which expressly includes an assignee of rents, a mortgagee in possession and a receiver. Do not expect loan or sale documents that assign rents to shift the repair duty away from whoever is collecting the rent.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to offer positive rent reporting, sets up a state rent-reporting program, bars requiring a tenant to join one, or sets a landlord-specific notice before you report unpaid rent to a credit bureau. If you or a vendor report rent payments, the general state and federal credit-reporting laws govern accuracy and disputes, and charging the tenant for a reporting service at or before move-in would be a barred upfront fee. Screening-report duties are in `edu-tenant-screening-ny` and `edu-fcra-adverse-action-notice`.

title: Government Inspections of Rental Housing
bodyText: New York State has no general rental-permit or rental-inspection program, and no statute lets a lease give a housing inspector the tenant's consent to enter. State laws do give officials their own inspection powers: local boards of health may enter and inspect premises where a nuisance or health hazard is known or believed to exist, and owners, agents and occupants must permit those sanitary inspections; in cities under 325,000 and in all towns and villages, the officer who enforces the Multiple Residence Law, and fire inspectors assigned under it, may enter and inspect buildings it covers; and, outside New York City, the local governments that enforce the state Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code must, under the Department of State's rules, inspect multiple dwellings for fire safety and property maintenance at least every three years (every year for a building with an assembly area for 50 or more people), must answer bona fide complaints with inspections where appropriate, and must tell the owner and operator how a building fails the code, citing the provisions; those rules do not require regular inspections of owner-occupied one- and two-family homes, though an inspector may still come at the owner's or occupant's invitation or where conditions threaten health or safety. Outside New York City, a pre-1980 building with two or more rental units in a community the Health Department names must be inspected and certified free of lead paint hazards at least every three years (`edu-lead-safe-certification-ny`). Many cities, towns and villages add their own rental permit and inspection laws, and New York City has its Housing Maintenance Code; these rows name local law but do not research it. Whether an inspector may enter without the tenant's consent or a warrant is a constitutional question, so don't treat the lease as consent: the `rental-inspection-cooperation-mn` clause asks the tenant to cooperate and to tell you of a refusal.

title: Repair Costs Are Not a Way Out of a New York Lease
bodyText: No New York statute lets you end a lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much, and none sets a cost threshold against the rent or the property's value, for you or the tenant; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. The warranty of habitability has no cost limit and cannot be waived, so expense is no defence to it. After a fire or other casualty, the tenant may leave under the casualty statute, and you may end the lease only if the lease gives you that right (the optional casualty clause does, where you reasonably decide not to restore). Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, a good-faith plan to demolish the building or withdraw it from the rental market is a ground for eviction only if you prove it by clear and convincing evidence in court; elsewhere a lease that has not ended still binds you.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption From Repair Remedies
bodyText: New York has no rule letting a small landlord opt out of tenants' repair remedies by giving notice: no statute exempts owners of a few units from the rent-deposit stay, the warranty of habitability or the repair proceedings because they told the tenant so; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. Where conditions are dangerous, a tenant in a nonpayment or rent case can ask the court to stay it by depositing the rent with the court clerk, and tenants can bring special proceedings for repair orders or an administrator (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ny`). A lease term waiving those rights is void (`edu-prohibited-terms-ny`).

title: No Statutory Repair-Notice Method in New York
bodyText: No New York statute prescribes how, or in what form, a tenant must ask you for repairs; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. The library's maintenance clause asks the tenant to tell you promptly in writing, which gives you a record, but that term cannot cut down the tenant's rights. The warranty of habitability cannot be waived or modified, and the statute does not make written notice a condition of the warranty or of a court stay, so a condition you learn of another way (by phone, from your own inspection or from an agency violation notice) can still count against you. A tenant's good-faith complaint to you, your agent or a government agency also starts the retaliation protections, whatever form it takes. Act on every report however it reaches you and keep a dated record; when notice matters to a remedy is case law, which was not searched.

title: Required New York Lease Disclosures
bodyText: Every New York residential lease must carry three state notices: the Good Cause Eviction Law notice, in the statute's own words, appended to or included in every initial and renewal lease (`good-cause-notice-ny`); a bold notice saying whether the unit has a maintained and operative sprinkler system and, if it does, the last date of maintenance and inspection (`sprinkler-disclosure-ny`); and the flood notice stating whether the premises are in a FEMA floodplain, the 100-year or the 500-year flood zone, any prior flood damage you know or should know of, and the statute's statement on renters' flood insurance (`flood-disclosure-ny`). Five more apply only in some cases: if you own three or fewer rental units, a bold notice before signing saying whether a required certificate of occupancy is currently valid (`certificate-of-occupancy-notice-ny`); if you put the deposit in a bank, written notice of the bank's name and address and the amount (`deposit-bank-notice-ny`); in a building with three or more households living independently, written notice about the emergency contact list and each resident's written consent to be on it (`emergency-contact-consent-ny`); in such a building outside New York City, written notice of the owner's and tenant's smoke detector duties (`smoke-detector-duties-ny`); and for a condominium unit, the unit particulars the Condominium Act requires in leases of units (`condo-unit-particulars-ny`). Two more apply only where a state environmental program reaches the property: where an engineering control or ongoing remedial monitoring addresses indoor air contamination and you have received test results, a bold notice of test results on the lease's first page, with the Department of Health fact sheet before signing (`indoor-air-test-notice-ny`); and where a recorded environmental easement held by the Department of Environmental Conservation affects the property, a reference to it in the lease and, as the cautious course, the statute's sentence that the property is subject to the easement in bold, at least 15-point type (`environmental-easement-ny`). If the lease or listing describes the property by the name of a different town or city (a nearby village name, for example), it must also name the place where the property actually is, just as prominently. Federal law adds the lead warning statement, your disclosure of known lead-based paint and records, the pamphlet and signed certifications for housing built before 1978 (`lead-based-paint`). Other state notices are given outside the lease: written notice of the right to request disability accommodations within 30 days after the tenancy starts, which the library puts in the lease (`accommodation-notice-ny`) and which must also be posted at the property and linked from the homepage of any website you maintain (`edu-accommodation-notice-ny`), bed bug notices during the tenancy (`edu-bed-bug-ny`), renewal and rent-increase notices (`edu-rent-increase-notice-ny`), and the deposit inspection offers (`edu-move-in-inspection-ny`). Rent-regulated units need their own riders (`edu-scope-ny`), and New York City and other localities add notices these rows name but do not research.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. Two narrower state notices do exist: the Good Cause Eviction Law notice that goes in every lease and renewal (`good-cause-notice-ny`), and a written notice of the right to request reasonable accommodations and modifications that state human rights regulations require within 30 days after a tenancy starts (`edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-ny`). Manufactured home park owners must include a state-approved tenant rights rider with park leases, but those park tenancies are outside these rows. New York City and other localities may require their own notices; these rows name local law but do not research it.

title: No Duty to Give Tenants a Code Variance
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a variance, exception or waiver from a health, building, fire or housing code; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. Variances exist: the Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code may be varied under a procedure the Secretary of State's rules must establish, a city board may vary the Multiple Dwelling Law, and county or local review boards may vary the Multiple Residence Law, each where strict compliance causes practical difficulty or unnecessary hardship (for the Uniform Code, also where it would otherwise be unwarranted) and safety is preserved. Those boards keep their decisions open to public inspection, but the law puts no notice duty on you. A tenant affected by a variance may still ask about it, so keep a copy with your building records. The State Sanitary Code, the Uniform Code's own variance rules and local rules (not researched here) may say more.

title: Seasonal Rentals
bodyText: New York has no separate law for seasonal tenancies: a summer or winter rental is an ordinary tenancy, and the usual rules apply, including the one-month deposit cap and its return within 14 days. A unit qualifies as a seasonal use dwelling unit only if all of these are true: the local government or county has a seasonal-use registry and the unit is registered in it; the lease expressly states the registration and the registering agency, that occupancy is for seasonal use of no more than 120 days (or a shorter stated period), and the address of the tenant's primary residence; and the unit is not rented as a seasonal unit for more than 120 days a year. A qualifying unit may take a deposit above one month's rent, and it is outside the Good Cause Eviction Law, but the library does not offer the seasonal deposit term, because these rows cover year-round residential leases; you may add your own clause meeting every condition above (`edu-deposit-rules-ny`). Stays of under 30 days are short-term rentals with their own registration rules (`edu-short-term-rental-ny`).

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease term in which the tenant waives the deposit law's protections is void. That covers the trust, bank-notice and interest rules, and the one-month cap, the closed list of deductions, the move-in and pre-move-out inspections, the 14-day itemized statement and the landlord's burden of proof. A void term does not bind the tenant, and keeping money under one can expose you to actual damages and, for a willful violation, punitive damages of up to twice the deposit (`edu-deposit-penalty-ny`, `edu-knowing-use-ny`). The Attorney General can also sue to compel compliance. See `edu-prohibited-terms-ny` and `edu-deposit-rules-ny`. Rent-controlled units and some senior-care facilities are outside the cap-and-inspection rules, and rent-stabilized units follow their own section (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: No Posted Deposit-Standards Rule
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to post or hand out the standards you use to set different tenants' security deposits, whatever the number of units. Every deposit and advance is still capped at one month's rent, and the standards you use must not treat applicants differently on a protected ground, including lawful source of income (`edu-fair-housing-ny`, `edu-source-of-income-ny`). Rent-stabilized units follow their own rules (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: No Staff Work Cards for Senior Housing
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires work cards, permits or background checks for staff who work in housing for people 55 or older (or 62 or older), or in any other ordinary rental housing; any screening of your employees follows general employment law, which these rows do not cover. What New York regulates is the housing itself: senior housing is exempt from the Human Rights Law's age and familial-status rules only if it is restricted to people 62 or older (and their spouses) or is intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit under the federal test, which requires at least 80% of occupied units to have such a resident, published age policies you follow, and age verification by reliable surveys and affidavits. Licensed care settings such as assisted living and adult care facilities have their own licensing rules and are outside these rows. The other fair housing rules still apply to senior housing (`edu-fair-housing-ny`).

title: No Sex Offender Registry Disclosure Duty
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to tell a tenant or applicant whether a registered sex offender lives in or near the property, or to put a registry notice in the lease. The state keeps a public internet subdirectory of level two and level three sex offenders, searchable by county and zip code, and a free telephone line for asking whether a named person is registered; anyone, including a tenant, can use them. Anyone who uses the subdirectory's information in violation of the law faces a fine of $500 to $1,000 on top of any other penalty, so do not use it to harass a tenant or neighbor. Whether you may screen applicants on a sex offense conviction is covered in `edu-no-sex-offender-rule-ny`; screening must still respect the Human Rights Law's limits on criminal-history inquiries (`edu-tenant-screening-ny`). A notice clause has no protective effect under New York law, so the library does not offer one.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice
bodyText: No New York statute requires a special notice, with a set type size or first-page placement, when you rent a single-family house, or a lease statement about presumptions of unlawful occupancy; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. New York handles unlawful occupants another way: a squatter, meaning someone who entered without permission and stays without right, is not a tenant, so the eviction-case protections for tenants do not cover them (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-ny`). A signed written lease is your best proof of who is lawfully in the house. The general format rules still apply to the whole lease (`edu-small-print-ny`).

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: No New York statute requires a lease of waterfront or shoreline property to disclose public access to the shore, beach rights or water-use restrictions; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. Limits on waterfront property come from deeds and recorded easements, association rules, state environmental permits and local waterfront and zoning rules, none of which these rows research. If the lease grants the tenant use of a dock, beach or shared waterfront, describe it in the lease so both sides know what is included. Flood history and flood-zone status must still be disclosed in every lease (`flood-disclosure-ny`).

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection in New York
bodyText: New York has no rent protection tied to a government shutdown: a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found nothing giving a federal or state employee extra time to pay rent, suspending late fees, pausing evictions during a lapse in appropriations, or shielding a furloughed tenant's utility service, and the Public Service Commission's residential utility rules have no such protection either. Rent stays due on the date the lease sets. The ordinary protections still apply to every tenant: no late fee until rent is more than five days late, capped at $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less; a written 14-day rent demand before any nonpayment case; and the court's power to stay an eviction for hardship. Offering a payment plan is your choice, and putting it in writing avoids disputes. Servicemembers on active duty have separate protections.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No New York statute limits renting a house in a single-family zone to owners who live on the lot, and New York has no state lot-split or two-unit program with its own owner-occupancy, short-term-letting or tenant-protection conditions; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. Zoning is local: cities, towns and villages regulate the use of buildings and land under their state zoning powers, and some local codes restrict rentals, short-term rentals or the number of unrelated occupants in residential districts. Check the zoning code where the property is before you rent; these rows name local law but do not research it.

title: Keyless and App-Based Entry
bodyText: New York has one statute on keyless entry: before a keyless system (such as a fob, card, app or biometric reader) is installed for the common areas of a residential building, the owner must give occupants at least 30 days' written notice, the system cannot be a reason to raise rent, and it must not obstruct how residents get into the building (`edu-security-devices-ny`). No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution regulates smart locks on the apartment door itself, requires you to offer a physical key instead of an app, or sets rules for entry logs, so those are lease terms (`smart-access-ny`). Never disable a tenant's code or fob to keep the tenant out: changing or disabling the entrance lock without giving the occupant a way in is unlawful eviction. If the system stores fingerprints or face data, New York's data breach and data security laws treat that biometric information as private information you must safeguard. New York City has its own law on smart-access systems in multiple dwellings, which these rows do not cover.

title: Secondhand Smoke Drift
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution addresses smoke drifting between apartments or lets a tenant waive claims about it, and the library does not offer a smoke-drift waiver. A lease term in which the tenant gives up the warranty of habitability is void, and so is a term excusing you from liability for your own negligence, so a waiver would protect you little if drifting smoke made an apartment unfit (a question for case law these rows do not research). The state Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking and vaping in places of employment, which it defines to include indoor hallways and elevators where an employer's staff work, but it does not apply to private homes and residences; whether it reaches the common areas of a particular apartment building is not settled in the statute. The better tool is a smoke-free policy (`smoking-policy-ny`): New York lets a smoke-free property bar smoking of cannabis as well as tobacco, but not certified medical use of cannabis.

title: Late Benefit or Subsidy Payments in a Nonpayment Case
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires the court to adjourn or reinstate a nonpayment case because a tenant's Social Security, public assistance or subsidy payment arrived late. Related rules do apply: the tenant may still pay the full rent before the hearing, or before the warrant is executed, and stop the case (`edu-redemption-ny`); a tenant on public assistance has a defense for any period when reported dangerous or hazardous violations were outstanding; in New York City the court may bring the city's social services department into the case, and a court-ordered rent deposit cannot include the subsidy share or more than 30% of a fixed income such as Social Security (`edu-rent-into-court-ny`); and the court may grant a hardship stay (`edu-eviction-stay-ny`). Refusing a tenant because their rent comes from a benefit or voucher is source-of-income discrimination (`edu-source-of-income-ny`).

title: No Special District Disclosure
bodyText: No New York statute requires a lease to tell the tenant that the property lies in a special improvement, taxing or assessment district (such as a town water, sewer or lighting district or a business improvement district), or to describe the tenant's role in one; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. District taxes and charges are levied against the property, not the tenant. You may take them into account in setting the rent, but a separate charge for them is limited: New York bars most fees at the start of a tenancy beyond rent and the deposit, and an eviction case can recover only rent (`edu-fees-as-rent-ny`).

title: New York's Money Caps at a Glance
bodyText: New York's state caps on what you may charge a market-rate tenant: all deposits and advances together, one month's rent; background and credit checks, the lesser of actual cost or $20 (waived if the applicant gives you a check from the past 30 days), and no other fee before or at the beginning of the tenancy; late fees, nothing until rent is five days late, then the lesser of $50 or 5% of the monthly rent; a dishonored rent check, only if the lease provides for it, and no more than the greater of your actual costs or $20; on an interest-bearing deposit account, an administration sum of 1% a year; and no legal, court or administrative fees without a court order. There is no statewide cap on rent for market-rate units, but where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, a yearly increase above the local rent standard (the lower of 10% or inflation plus 5%) is presumed unreasonable. A lease term exceeding a cap is void. Details are in `edu-deposit-rules-ny`, `edu-application-fee-ny`, `edu-late-fee-ny`, `returned-payments-ny`, `edu-deposit-interest-ny`, `edu-attorney-fees-ny` and `edu-rent-control-ny`; rent-regulated units follow their own rules (`edu-scope-ny`), and local law may add limits.

title: When a Tenant May End a Lease Early by Law
bodyText: New York lets a tenant end a lease before the term ends, whatever the lease says, in these cases: a domestic violence victim on 30 days' written notice with documentation (`edu-dv-termination-ny`); a tenant 62 or older or with a disability who is moving to a family member's home, a care facility or senior or subsidized housing (`edu-senior-termination-ny`); the estate of a tenant who dies, for leases made or renewed on or after February 15, 2024 (`edu-tenant-death-ny`); and a tenant who enters military service, under the Military Law and federal law (`edu-servicemember-ny`). A tenant may also leave and stop paying rent if the building is destroyed or made unfit to live in without the tenant's fault, unless a written agreement says otherwise (`edu-casualty-ny`). Each exit has its own notice, timing and rent rules; a lease cannot cut them down, and any early-termination option you offer must leave them intact. A tenant's right to end a lease for your fraud or misrepresentation would come from case law, which the library did not search.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to put covers on steam radiators or hot pipes, to offer them on request, or to add a radiator-cover rider to the lease. Your general duty to keep the apartment fit and free of conditions dangerous to life, health or safety still applies (`edu-habitability-ny`), and, outside New York City, the state Property Maintenance Code, which applies to all existing buildings and premises, and local codes (for example, New York City's) may reach heating equipment; these rows do not hold the Property Maintenance Code's text. If a household has young children or a tenant asks, covering exposed steam radiators and risers is a cautious step.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
