bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator in a market-rate rental. The state Multiple Dwelling and Multiple Residence Laws regulate cooking spaces (kitchens and kitchenettes must meet fire-safety rules, and, under the Multiple Dwelling Law, which applies in New York City, other cities of 325,000 or more and localities that adopt it, a gas cooking appliance may not be used in a room for living or sleeping unless the room has a window to the outer air or the appliance is vented outdoors) but do not say who supplies the appliances. Outside New York City, the state Property Maintenance Code applies to all existing buildings and premises and may set food-preparation requirements for dwelling units; its text is a model-code publication these rows do not hold, and local codes may require appliances. If you apply to submeter electricity, the Public Service Commission asks for proof that the refrigerators in all rental units are no more than 10 years old or meet the latest federal efficiency standards (a filing rule amended in 2025 whose current text these rows could not read; `edu-electric-submetering-ny`). If you supply appliances, list them in the lease (`appliances-included`) and keep them working as part of your repair duty (`edu-habitability-ny`).

title: Student Housing and Dormitories
bodyText: New York has no separate student-housing law: an apartment rented to students is an ordinary tenancy, and the usual deposit, fee, repair, notice and fair housing rules apply, whether or not the tenants are students. New York's rules for dormitories are exemptions, not duties. The Good Cause Eviction Law, where it applies, does not cover a dormitory owned and operated by a college, university or K-12 school, so a privately owned or master-leased student building remains covered unless another exemption applies (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`). In a multiple dwelling covered by the Multiple Dwelling Law (cities of 325,000 or more and places that adopt it), every tenant may add their own small lock to the apartment's entrance door (giving you a duplicate key on request) without any fee, except in a hotel, motel or college or school dormitory. You may rent all rooms in a unit to people of the same sex, but otherwise you may not choose among student applicants by any protected trait (`edu-fair-housing-ny`). Local student-housing or rooming-house rules are named, not researched.

title: Voucher Inspections and Source-of-Income Discrimination
bodyText: No New York statute mentions a landlord refusing a housing-subsidy inspection, but refusing a tenancy because a voucher needs one is risky. You may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, an applicant because of a lawful source of income, which includes Section 8 and any other housing assistance whether or not it is paid to you directly, and you may not use listings, applications or inquiries that express such a limitation. The only exemptions are an owner-occupied two-family building and rooms rented in the owner's own home. Whether refusing to let the program inspect, or to sign its contract, counts as refusing because of source of income is not settled by the statute or by the Division of Human Rights' rules read for these rows, and case law was not searched, so the cautious course is to cooperate with the inspection as you would with any other part of screening. New York's state Housing Access Voucher pilot program uses the federal voucher inspection standards, and local laws, including New York City's, may say more.

title: Subsidized Tenants and Habitability Abatements
bodyText: No New York statute sets how a habitability rent abatement is split between a subsidized tenant's share and the agency's share; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. For a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules decide most of it: the tenant is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, and if the housing agency withholds or abates that payment because you did not fix inspection deficiencies in time, you may not end the tenancy because of it, and abated payments are not made up later. The tenant's own share is still rent under New York law, so the warranty of habitability can reduce it for conditions you must fix. Where a public welfare official pays a recipient's rent, New York lets the official withhold it while a reported violation dangerous to life or health is outstanding, and you cannot evict or win a money judgment for that period.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Payment Is Late
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution sets a special late-fee rule for rent paid by a housing subsidy or agency. The ordinary cap applies to the tenant's own share: no late fee until it is more than five days late, then no more than $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less. Do not charge the tenant a late fee because an agency paid its share late. Under a federal Housing Choice Voucher contract the family is not responsible for the agency's share and the agency's late payment is not a lease violation, and charging tenants with subsidies fees others do not pay can be source-of-income discrimination (`edu-source-of-income-ny`). If you hold a voucher contract, follow its terms (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`).

title: Court Administrators and Receivers for Substandard Buildings
bodyText: If dangerous conditions go unfixed, New York law lets a court take over your rents to pay for the repairs. In New York City and Nassau, Suffolk, Rockland and Westchester counties, one-third of the tenants (or, in New York City, the housing agency) can bring a rent deposit proceeding for a lack of heat, water, light, electricity or sewage disposal or another dangerous condition lasting five days, rodent infestation, or harassment; elsewhere the same proceeding is open to one-third of the tenants of a multiple residence, a single tenant of a one-unit dwelling, or the local code agency. The court can order all tenants to pay rent to an administrator it appoints, who uses it to make the repairs and turns any surplus over to you; while the order is in effect, the warranty of habitability is no defence to the administrator's claims for rent. You have defences if the condition did not exist or was fixed, was caused by tenants, their families or guests, or a tenant refused you entry. Where the Multiple Dwelling Law applies, the housing department can also ask a court to appoint a receiver of the rents to remove a nuisance, with a lien for the cost ranking ahead of mortgages. Local code liens and in rem foreclosure are local law, not researched here.

title: Ending a Tenancy at Will or by Sufferance
bodyText: A tenancy at will (an occupancy with your permission and no set term or rent period) or by sufferance (staying on without permission after a right to occupy ended), however created, ends on your written notice of at least 30 days requiring the tenant to leave. Serve it by handing it to the tenant or to a person of suitable age and discretion living there, or, if neither can be found, by posting it on a conspicuous part of the premises. The statute says you may then re-enter, but an occupant who has lived there 30 days or more, or has a lease, may be removed only through a summary proceeding, and self-help is unlawful (`edu-unlawful-eviction-ny`). Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, you also need a good-cause ground (`edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`). See `edu-termination-notice-ny` for the notices other tenancies need.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Federal bankruptcy law controls once a tenant files: the filing automatically stays most acts to take possession, so stop the eviction case and any warrant unless an exception applies or the bankruptcy court lifts the stay. The stay does not stop an eviction where you got a judgment for possession before the filing, but the tenant can delay that for 30 days by certifying that New York law lets them cure the money default after judgment (it does, by paying all rent due before the warrant is executed) and depositing 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk, and can stop it by curing within those 30 days; it also does not stop an eviction based on endangering the property or illegal drug use if you file the required certification. The lease cannot be ended just because the tenant filed or is insolvent, and in a Chapter 7 case a residential lease the trustee does not assume within 60 days is deemed rejected. New York's eviction statute still lists a tenant's bankruptcy under a lease of three years or less as a ground for eviction, but federal law overrides it while the case is open, so do not rely on it. Get bankruptcy advice before acting.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Private
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution generally bars a landlord from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information, or sets a consent rule for doing so. Specific rules do apply: you must keep confidential everything learned when a tenant ends a lease because of domestic violence and may not describe it as an early termination to anyone, unless the tenant authorizes release in writing or the law or a court requires it (`edu-dv-confidentiality-ny`); you may not intentionally make a person's Social Security number available to the public, print it on mailed materials, or require it to be sent over an unsecured internet connection; and court records of a tenant removed after a foreclosure are sealed (`edu-eviction-records-ny`). You also may not use information about a person's immigration status, or any other protected trait, to refuse to rent or set different terms (`edu-fair-housing-ny`). How you must secure the Social Security, license and bank numbers you collect, and what to do after a data breach, is in `edu-tenant-records-ny`. Local privacy laws, such as New York City's rules on smart access systems, are named, not researched.

title: Housing an Employee
bodyText: New York requires no special disclosure or form when you house an employee, such as a superintendent, but two rules turn on whether the housing is only incident to the job. First, you may bring an eviction case against a person who took possession as an incident to employment by you once the agreed time for possession has expired or, if none was agreed, once the employment ends, without first serving a notice to quit. Second, where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, it does not protect a unit occupied solely incident to employment once that employment is being or has been lawfully ended, and your renewal notice must say so if that is the reason. If you use `employee-housing-ny`, state the job and how many days after the job ends the right to occupy ends; you must still go to court, never lock the person out, and return the deposit under the deposit law. Whether an employee who pays rent under a full lease is treated as a tenant instead turns on case law, so get legal advice before relying on the shortcut.

title: Fire, Casualty and Insurance Claims
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution shields a tenant from liability for an accidental fire, governs claims between your insurer and the tenant, or authorizes a lease clause in which you and the tenant release each other from insured losses. A tenant who negligently damages the property is answerable for it, and in a Multiple Dwelling Law or Multiple Residence Law building is liable for a violation caused by the tenant's, a household member's or a guest's wilful act or negligence. If the unit is destroyed or made unfit by fire or another cause without the tenant's fault, and the lease does not say otherwise in writing, the tenant may move out and stop owing rent from then on (`edu-casualty-ny`). The library offers no mutual waiver or release clause: any lease term exempting you from liability for your own negligence is void, and whether a release tied to insurance escapes that rule is a question for the courts.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText: You may offer an online portal for rent, maintenance requests and documents (`tenant-portal-il`), but New York does not let you make electronic billing or payment the only way to pay rent, or charge any fee to a tenant who chooses not to use it; a lease term giving up that right is void (`acceptable-payment-methods-ny`). Electronic signatures and records have the same effect as handwritten and paper ones, but no one can be required to use them unless another law says so, so let the tenant sign on paper if the tenant asks. A notice the law says must be served or mailed in a particular way, such as a rent demand, a late-rent notice by certified mail or a termination notice, must still go that way even if you also post it to the portal (`electronic-notice-ny`). Keep the portal's data secure, because tenant financial account information is private information under New York's data security law.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires you to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant one on request, or attach one to a rent demand. Two record duties do apply: you must give written rent receipts for cash and non-check payments (and for checks if the tenant asks in writing) and keep records of cash receipts for at least three years (`edu-rent-receipts-ny`), and you must send a certified-mail notice if rent is not received within five days of its due date (`edu-late-fee-ny`). New York's data security law does reach you if you keep computerized records with a tenant's or applicant's Social Security number, driver's license number, bank or card account number with its access code, or similar private information: you must keep reasonable administrative, technical and physical safeguards (scaled to a small business's size), dispose of the data when no longer needed, and notify affected New Yorkers of a breach as quickly as possible and within 30 days of discovery. Paper and electronic records with those numbers must be shredded, destroyed or made unreadable before disposal. Keeping an accurate ledger anyway is good practice, because in a nonpayment case you must prove what is owed.

title: Agreements for Tenant-Performed Repairs in New York
bodyText: New York has no statute on agreements for a tenant to do repairs or chores: no separate-document rule, no consideration requirement and no limit to single-family homes, so an agreement for specified tasks binds as an ordinary lease term or rider in any kind of dwelling; a search of the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution found none. The limit is the warranty of habitability, which cannot be waived or modified: the tenant can take on chores and minor upkeep, but any repair needed to keep the home fit to live in stays yours. In a multiple dwelling you also stay responsible to the authorities for repair and cleanliness, whatever the tenant agrees. Use the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement clause, list each task specifically, and state anything you give in return.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: New York has no state-agency statement or summary of tenant rights that must be attached to a lease or signed by the tenant, and no statute bars a suit until one is given; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The nearest analogue is the Good Cause Eviction Law notice, whose text the statute prescribes and which must be appended to or included in every initial and renewal lease, and in certain notices and eviction petitions, whether or not the unit is covered (`good-cause-notice-ny`). Separately, the Division of Human Rights' rules require every housing provider to give each tenant a written notice, within 30 days after the tenancy starts, of the right to request reasonable modifications and accommodations for a disability, in 12-point type or larger and with the phone number and e-mail of the person who takes requests; the rules print a model notice, which may go in or with the lease, and you must also post it at the property and link to it from the homepage of any website you maintain. The same rules require you, if your housing is subject to the Human Rights Law, to post and keep up, conspicuously at your housing, the Division's notice summarizing the Human Rights Law's housing provisions and where to file a complaint. Neither notice has to be attached to the lease or signed by the tenant. Manufactured home park leases need a state-approved tenant rights rider, but those park tenancies are outside these rows, and New York City and other localities may add notices that these rows name but do not research.

title: Notice Before Changing Lease Terms
bodyText: During a fixed term you cannot change the lease without the tenant's agreement (building rules adopted under `rules-ny` aside). To change terms when a lease or month-to-month tenancy renews, two state rules apply. If you will offer renewal with a rent increase of 5% or more, or will not renew, you must give written notice 30, 60 or 90 days ahead depending on how long the tenant has lived there or the lease length, whichever is longer, with the Good Cause Eviction Law notice; if you are late, the tenancy continues on its existing terms until the full period has run from your actual notice (`edu-rent-increase-notice-ny`). Where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, a tenant's refusal of reasonable changes at renewal is good cause only if you gave written notice of the changes 30 to 90 days before the lease expired. No New York statute sets a separate or longer notice for raising a fee or changing other terms of a periodic tenancy; give the same written notice for every change as a matter of practice. Ending a month-to-month tenancy is covered in `edu-termination-notice-ny`.

title: Stating a Good Cause Exemption
bodyText: If your unit is exempt from the Good Cause Eviction Law, you say so in the same statutory notice that goes in every lease and renewal: question 2 of the form lists each exemption to mark (for example, a place outside New York City that has not opted in, a small landlord, an owner-occupied building of 10 units or fewer, a regulated or income-restricted unit, a condominium or co-op unit, a newer building, a seasonal unit, or a high-rent unit) (`good-cause-notice-ny`). There is no separate exemption notice to give. If you later rely on the small-landlord exemption in an eviction case, you must disclose the natural persons who own the property and the units they own, in the petition and to the tenant. The exemptions themselves are explained in `edu-for-cause-eviction-ny`.

title: Tenant Protection Notice in New York
bodyText: New York's counterpart to a tenant protection act notice is the Good Cause Eviction Law notice: every initial and renewal lease, and every renewal, non-renewal or 5%-plus rent increase notice, must append or include the statutory form saying whether the unit is covered and, if not, why (`good-cause-notice-ny`). New York has no separate statewide rent-cap notice; the Good Cause Eviction Law instead presumes increases above the local rent standard unreasonable where it applies (`edu-rent-control-ny`). New York also gives ordinary residential tenants no right to buy or to be offered the building when you sell; manufactured home park residents and tenants in a co-op or condominium conversion have their own purchase rights, outside these rows (`edu-conversion-ny`).

title: Tenant Protections With Repeal Dates
bodyText: New York's Good Cause Eviction Law, and the notice that goes with it, are set to be repealed on June 15, 2034: on that date the good-cause rules, the local rent standard presumption, the statutory lease notice (`good-cause-notice-ny`) and the extra items in eviction petitions drop away, and the renewal and rent-increase notice law switches to a version that no longer includes the Good Cause notice (`edu-rent-increase-notice-ny`). The state lead rental registry and certification law outside New York City is set to be repealed on November 3, 2028 (`edu-lead-safe-certification-ny`). The other landlord-tenant protections these rows rely on, such as the warranty of habitability, the deposit and fee limits and the anti-retaliation law, have no repeal date. The Legislature can extend or change any of these dates, so check before relying on one.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: No New York statute requires you to translate a market-rate residential lease or its required notices, even if you advertised or negotiated in another language, and New York has no rule on competing official-language texts of its laws; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. The one translation rule near a lease is in the home equity theft law: when a homeowner in default or foreclosure sells to an equity purchaser and rents or leases the home back, the covered contract (which must state the rental or lease terms) and its cancellation notice must be in 12-point bold type, in English or in both English and Spanish if Spanish is the seller's primary language. Rent-regulation and public-housing forms come in several languages, but those units are outside these rows. If a tenant reads English poorly, offering a translation is good practice, but the English lease is what you sign. New York City and other localities may have language-access rules these rows do not research.

title: Barring Non-Tenants Under the Trespass Law
bodyText: New York's Penal Law makes it trespass to knowingly enter or remain unlawfully on premises, meaning without a license or privilege, and a more serious crime to do so in a dwelling or in a fenced or enclosed building; in a public housing project it is also a crime to break posted entry rules or ignore a request to leave from a housing police officer or other person in charge. A person in a part of a building open to the public is licensed to be there until they defy a lawful order to leave personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person, and a license to enter the public part does not cover the private part. No statute sets a landlord's written trespass-notice procedure for a private rental building, and a person a tenant invites may be there on the tenant's license, so barring a tenant's guest is a question for case law; give any order to leave in person, keep a record, and let the police decide whether to charge. You may not use a trespass notice to limit who lives in the unit beyond the roommate law (`permitted-occupants-ny`, `guest-policy-ny`), to punish a call for police or emergency help (`edu-emergency-assistance-ny`), or to remove a tenant or occupant without a court case (`edu-unauthorized-occupant-ny`).

title: No Truth in Renting Act
bodyText: New York has no Truth in Renting Act: no state agency statement of rights must be given to tenants, and no required lease notice tells tenants that the lease must comply with such an act; this was checked against the Consolidated Laws of New York and the New York Constitution. New York reaches the same ground through separate rules: the plain-language law (`edu-plain-language-ny`), the list of lease terms that are void (`edu-prohibited-terms-ny`), the consumer protection law (`edu-consumer-protection-ny`) and the Good Cause Eviction Law notice that goes in every lease (`good-cause-notice-ny`).

title: Leasing When You Hold Only a Life Estate
bodyText: New York has no usufruct; the closest interest is a life estate, which lasts for your life or another person's. No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York says that a lease made by a life tenant ends when the life estate ends or requires you to tell the tenant you hold only a life estate, but when it ends the person next entitled to the property (the remainderman or reversioner) may bring an eviction case against your tenant who stays on, so the tenant's rights may end with yours. If you die between rent days, your estate may recover the rent that accrued before your death. A will or deed may give a life tenant a power to make leases of up to 21 years that bind the later owners; a longer lease under the power is void as to the excess. If you hold only a life estate, tell the tenant in the lease and consider having the remainder holders sign it; get advice, because whether your lease binds them is otherwise a question of case law.

title: Utility Allowances and Rebilling Limits
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility you pay and rebill, or regulates a monthly utility allowance with a tenant-paid overage. If you offer an allowance, use it only for a utility-owned meter that serves the apartment alone and bill the tenant no more than the provider's actual charge above the allowance (`utility-allowance-cap-mi`). If you submeter electricity, the Public Service Commission's rules cap what you charge at what the utility would charge a similar directly metered residential customer for delivery and supply in that billing period, and bar time-of-use rates the tenant has not agreed to (`edu-electric-submetering-ny`); and once a shared meter's charges have been moved to your account you may never bill the tenant any share of them, though the statute still lets you raise future rent by a specific sum where the law otherwise allows (`edu-utility-apportionment-ny`). For the state utility tax, a landlord's receipts from reselling utilities to tenants are treated as equal to the landlord's cost. In a manufactured home park, utility charges must be reasonably related to services actually rendered, disclosed in writing before the rental agreement, and raised only on 90 days' written notice.

title: Shared Meters and Splitting Utility Bills
bodyText: New York regulates one kind of utility split by statute: a shared meter. If a gas, electric or steam meter on your tenant's own utility account also measures service outside the apartment (hallway lights, a boiler, another unit), you must either eliminate the shared meter or open an account in your own name for that service; you may instead sign a written agreement with the tenant only if a legal restriction prevents separate metering, the work would cost more than four months' rent, or the outside use is minimal under Public Service Commission rules, and then the tenant may pay only for the estimated service to the apartment (`shared-meter-agreement-ny`). The utility investigates on a tenant's complaint, can move the account into your name, refunds the tenant, and in most cases bills you for twelve months of the shared meter's charges; you may not bill the tenant for refunded charges or for any share of later bills in your name, though you may raise rent by a specific sum where the law otherwise allows. These rules cannot be waived by you or the tenant, and a lease renewal counts as a new lease. Splitting a master-metered bill you pay yourself among tenants (ratio billing) is not addressed by any New York statute or by the Commission's electric submetering rules; electric submetering is governed by the Commission's rules, which forbid any shared meter or cross-wiring in a submetered building (`edu-electric-submetering-ny`), and charges the lease makes payable to you are not rent (`edu-utility-submetering-ny`).

title: Utility Deposits Held by the Landlord
bodyText: New York has no separate rule for a utility deposit you collect yourself. Money you take as security for utility charges is a deposit or advance: it counts toward the one-month cap on all deposits and advances, is held in trust, and is refunded with the security deposit within 14 days after the tenant vacates, with an itemized statement. You may keep from it only what the law lists, which includes unpaid utility charges that the lease makes payable directly to you. Those charges are not rent, so you cannot recover them in an eviction case; collect them from the deposit or in an ordinary suit. Deposits a utility company takes from your tenant for the tenant's own account are the company's business under the Public Service Law. If you submeter electricity, the Public Service Commission's submetering rules make you follow the Home Energy Fair Practices Act and its rules, which bar requiring a deposit from a new residential customer as a condition of service except from seasonal or short-term customers or as the Commission authorizes; whether a submetered tenant counts as such a customer is not settled in the rules, so the cautious course is not to take a separate electricity deposit from a submetered tenant (`edu-electric-submetering-ny`, `edu-utility-submetering-ny`).

title: Heating and Cooling Bills for Prospective Tenants
bodyText: New York's truth-in-heating law applies when you offer a house, a two-family home or an apartment for rent to the public and the tenant will pay the heating or cooling bills. If a prospective tenant asks, you must immediately furnish a complete set of the heating and cooling bills, or a summary, for the past two years (or the life of the building if shorter), showing whether the unit was occupied during each period. You may not charge for this, and you may not reveal a past tenant's name without that tenant's consent; if you lack the bills, ask the utility or fuel vendor, which must send copies within ten days. The duty is to furnish the records on request, not to attach them to the lease, and a violation can bring a civil penalty of up to $100 but does not void the lease. Who pays which utility is set in the lease itself (`utilities-responsibility`, `utilities-paid-by-landlord`).

title: Getting Notice of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff
bodyText: New York utilities must let a residential customer name a third party, such as you, to receive copies of termination and collection notices and of past-due amounts and payments on the customer's account, if the third party agrees in writing to receive them; the customer can keep getting the notices too. Agreeing does not make you liable for the tenant's service, the utility must tell you so, and if you refuse or later cancel, the utility must promptly tell the tenant. A utility must also let a landlord name a third party to be told of every request to discontinue service to a tenant's apartment, but only on the written request of both the landlord and the tenant. The optional `utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co` clause has the tenant sign whatever form the provider requires, and you sign to accept the notices. Separately, before shutting off service to a whole building of three or more apartments, or to a two-family house without separate meters, the utility must notify every occupant (`edu-utility-landlord-account-ny`).

title: Cutting Off Submetered or Landlord-Supplied Utilities
bodyText: No New York statute expressly lets a landlord shut off electricity, gas or water it submeters or supplies to a tenant because the tenant has not paid; for electricity you submeter, the Public Service Commission's submetering rules make you follow the Home Energy Fair Practices Act, whose termination rules reach any entity that sells or helps sell electricity to residential customers, so a shutoff is possible only as described below. Shutting off or interrupting essential services to make a tenant leave is unlawful eviction, a crime that also carries a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000 for each violation; wilfully failing to furnish light, power or other services the lease requires is a separate violation; and in a multiple dwelling an owner who causes a shutoff by not paying the utility owes affected tenants compensatory and punitive damages. If you submeter electricity, the Public Service Commission's submetering rules require you to comply with the Home Energy Fair Practices Act and give your tenants its protections. Submetering authorized since 2016 (unless filed before 2014), and any later replacement system, must be able to shut off a single apartment, but only where the Act would allow a shutoff, so the rules contemplate cutting a submetered tenant's electricity for nonpayment only after the Act's notices and protections, and never to make the tenant leave. If your system cannot shut off a single apartment, you must still give the tenant every protection the Act would give a directly metered customer before you start any lawsuit, collection or other proceeding over the unpaid electricity. Gas and water you supply are outside the submetering rules; whether the Act's termination rules reach gas you resell is not settled (`edu-electric-submetering-ny`), and nothing read authorizes you to cut water, so do not cut either for nonpayment. Collect unpaid utility charges from the deposit or in an ordinary suit, not by cutting service (`edu-utility-submetering-ny`); short shutoffs for repairs should be announced and kept as brief as the work allows.

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: When gas, electric, steam or water service to a building is in your name and you fall behind, New York protects the tenants. Before shutting off service to an entire multiple dwelling (three or more apartments) for nonpayment, the utility must give 15 days' written notice posted in the public areas and mailed to the occupant of each apartment and to local officials, stating how tenants may pay to avoid the shutoff; for gas, electric and steam service, Public Service Commission rules require the mailed notices at least 18 days ahead, and 30 days ahead for heat-related service between November 1 and April 15, and the notice must tell tenants they may deduct their payments from rent. In a two-family house where service is not metered separately, each occupied unit must get 15 days' notice, and the utility must also post it at the house unless that is physically impossible. Under the Commission's rules for gas, electric and steam service, a multiple dwelling's service may not be shut off while the tenants keep making timely payments under the utility's approved procedure, and the utility may ask them for no more than the current charges for the latest billing period, not your earlier arrears; in a two-family house, an occupant who pays current charges (on monthly billing, up to the last two months' bills) is not liable for future bills. A tenant who lawfully pays the utility may deduct the payment from future rent, eviction cases and rent actions are stayed while service is off for your nonpayment, and in a multiple dwelling you can owe affected tenants compensatory and punitive damages (`edu-utility-shutoff-ny`). If service stays off for five days, one-third of the tenants (or, outside New York City and the four suburban counties, the tenant of a single-family rental) can ask a court to have rents paid into court and used to restore it (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-ny`).

title: Tenant Utility Transfers and No Cutoff Right
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution sets a deadline for a tenant to move utility accounts into the tenant's name or lets you shut off service in your name that the tenant failed to transfer. Put the transfer duty and a reimbursement of the provider's actual charges in the lease (`utility-transfer-nj`), and collect unpaid amounts from the deposit or in an ordinary suit; they are not rent. Do not end service to make the point: interrupting essential services to push a tenant out is unlawful eviction (`edu-unlawful-eviction-ny`), and in a building of three or more apartments, or a two-family house without separate meters, the utility must notify every occupant before a shutoff for your account's nonpayment (`edu-utility-landlord-account-ny`). A tenant who is a domestic violence victim may, by a written attestation, ask to be released from a shared utility contract without a fee, and the utility must release them no later than seven days after the request, so the account holder may change during the lease. New York law gives no utility-suspension right tied to military deployment.

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a landlord a tax credit, grant, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans. The closest program, Access to Home for Heroes, funds cities, towns, villages and nonprofits that give grants to low- and moderate-income disabled veterans, renters as well as homeowners, to adapt their homes; it pays for the work, not the landlord, and does not cover improvements you are already required by law to make. Military status is a protected class in New York housing, so you may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, someone because of military service, and you must accept veterans' housing assistance such as HUD-VASH vouchers as a lawful source of income (`edu-fair-housing-ny`). Unlike some states, New York's Human Rights Law has no exception allowing a rent discount or other concession offered only to veterans, so the library does not offer a veteran-concession clause; you may add your own, but have a New York lawyer review it first. Veteran preferences in state-supervised limited-profit (Mitchell-Lama) housing are regulated housing outside these rows (`edu-scope-ny`).

title: Hot Water and Water Heater Settings
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution sets a temperature for hot water or requires you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in. State law does require hot water itself in many buildings: where the Multiple Dwelling Law applies, buildings three or more stories high erected since April 18, 1929, and all multiple dwellings erected after January 1, 1951, must have hot and cold water at all hours all year; where the Multiple Residence Law applies, multiple dwellings erected on or after July 1, 1952 must have hot water from 6 a.m. to midnight. Outside New York City, minimum and maximum water temperatures, if any, are set by the 2020 Plumbing Code (for detached one- and two-family homes and townhouses, the 2020 Residential Code instead) and the 2020 Property Maintenance Code of New York State, which the state Uniform Code adopts by reference; these rows do not hold those codes' text. Local codes may also set them. A cautious practice is to check the setting at each turnover so the water is hot enough for use but not hot enough to scald.

title: Waterbeds and Water-Filled Furniture
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution gives a tenant a right to a waterbed or limits your rules on water-filled furniture, so the lease decides. The library's common-area rule already bars a waterbed or other water-filled furniture without your written consent (`common-area-use`), and the optional waterbed clause (`waterbed-mn`) sets the conditions if you consent, such as a proper frame and liner, an approved location and the tenant's own insurance against water damage. Apply the rule the same way to every tenant, and consider a reasonable accommodation if a tenant with a disability needs such a bed.

title: Window Guards and Window Bars
bodyText: No section of the Consolidated Laws of New York or the New York Constitution requires window guards for children, a window-guard lease notice or a window-fall rule. New York City has its own window-guard rule in its Health Code (section 131.15), local law these rows name but do not research, and other localities may have their own rules. State law does limit security bars: where the Multiple Dwelling Law applies, bars, grilles or gates on a window giving access to a fire escape or a required second exit are unlawful unless of an approved type installed as prescribed (in New York City, as the fire commissioner prescribes), and on a window or door to a required egress balcony in newer buildings they are unlawful; where the Multiple Residence Law applies, bars, grilles or gates on any window or door giving access to a fire escape are unlawful. Before you install guards or bars, check the local code and keep every fire-escape and emergency-exit window openable from inside.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: New York's statutes require many landlord notices to be in writing, and an oral notice does not satisfy them: the 14-day rent demand before a nonpayment case, the certified-mail notice when rent is five days late, the notice of non-renewal or of a rent increase of 5% or more, the notice ending a month-to-month tenancy in New York City, the 30-day notice ending a tenancy at will, and, where the Good Cause Eviction Law applies, the notice to cease a lease violation. Many tenant exits also run on the tenant's written notice, such as the domestic violence, senior and military terminations (`edu-statutory-early-termination-ny`). Each notice has its own delivery method, which the lease cannot replace (`edu-notice-service-ny`), and the library's `notices` clause defers to those rules. Put every notice in writing and keep proof of delivery.

title: Notice of the Right to Request Accommodations
bodyText: Every owner, managing agent, sublandlord or other housing provider in New York must give each tenant a written notice of the right to request reasonable modifications and reasonable accommodations for a disability, within 30 days after the tenancy begins. Tenants already in place when the law took effect on March 2, 2021 were due it within 30 days after that date; if you have tenants who never got it, for example in a building you bought, the cautious course is to give it to them now. The notice must be in writing, in 12-point type or larger (or another easily legible type), and must give the telephone number and e-mail address of the property manager or other person who accepts accommodation requests. You may deliver it by e-mail, text, electronic messaging, fax or on paper, and you may include it in or with the lease or other papers you routinely give tenants; on paper it must be in the document itself or in an accompanying one. A message that only links to the notice is enough if it says the link is about tenants' rights to reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities, and the notice must be printable and downloadable. Telling the tenant orally does not count, and neither does posting the notice. Posting is a separate duty: you must also post the notice conspicuously at the property, in an easily accessible, well-lighted place where people seeking housing can readily see it, and any website you create and maintain as a housing provider must prominently display on its homepage a link to the Division of Human Rights' notice. Separately, you must post the Division of Human Rights' notice of the Human Rights Law at your rental office or property, where it can be seen. The model notice printed in the Division's regulation is deemed sufficient; `accommodation-notice-ny` puts it in the lease. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson handles your listing, the broker must see that the notice goes to prospective tenants at the first substantive contact. The regulation states no exemption; whether the Human Rights Law's exemptions for an owner-occupied two-family house and for rooms in an owner's home carry over is unsettled, so the cautious course is to give the notice anyway. The rights themselves are in `edu-disability-accommodation-ny`. Local laws may add notices that these rows do not research.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: New York did not adopt the uniform rule on checks marked 'paid in full': its Uniform Commercial Code has no section 3-311, so whether cashing such a check settles a disputed claim is a matter of case law, which this library has not reviewed. New York's reservation-of-rights rule says a party that performs, or accepts performance, 'with explicit reservation of rights' does not prejudice the rights reserved, using words such as 'without prejudice' or 'under protest' (N.Y. U.C.C. § 1-308); unlike the uniform version, New York's says nothing to exclude an accord and satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it. If you do cash one, write an explicit reservation of rights with your endorsement (for example 'under protest, without prejudice to the balance owed') and keep a copy, knowing that its effect rests on case law.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: New York's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Real Property Law article 7 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how New York's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
